text: Whatever the impact of the smallpox epidemic on the KhoeKhoe of the southwestern Cape, it is clear that most KhoeKhoe to the north and east were not touched by the disease. And yet the decline and subjugation of these people by marauding colonists continued without pause. Europeans were able to gain a stranglehold on the lands they occupied, undercutting the very basis of KhoeKhoe livelihood. The exact mechanism of the process is set out above, and we believe it provides a plausible non-catastrophic explanation, beginning around 1706, of the gradual decline of the KhoeKhoe as independent peoples. Why did the KhoeKhoe put up such a weak resistance to European encroachment of their lands after the defeat of Gonnema in 1678? Shula Marks has sought to chronicle that resistance and has assembled considerable evidence to show that KhoeKhoe, as opposed to the San, did actively resist the advance of the European frontier.  53. Marks, Resistancepp.70-73.  * This resistance, however, proved feeble and KhoeKhoe accommodation to the settlers' society was the order of the day. The pattern of accommodation and sporadic resistance, it seems to us, is well explained by the gradual way in which Europeans infiltrated KhoeKhoe land one spring or spruijt at a time.
html: Whatever the impact of the smallpox epidemic on the KhoeKhoe of the southwestern Cape, it is clear that most KhoeKhoe to the north and east were not touched by the disease. And yet the decline and subjugation of these people by marauding colonists continued without pause. Europeans were able to gain a stranglehold on the lands they occupied, undercutting the very basis of KhoeKhoe livelihood. The exact mechanism of the process is set out above, and we believe it provides a plausible non-catastrophic explanation, beginning around 1706, of the gradual decline of the KhoeKhoe as independent peoples. Why did the KhoeKhoe put up such a weak resistance to European encroachment of their lands after the defeat of Gonnema in 1678? Shula Marks has sought to chronicle that resistance and has assembled considerable evidence to show that KhoeKhoe, as opposed to the San, did actively resist the advance of the European frontier.53. Marks, Resistancepp.70-73.* This resistance, however, proved feeble and KhoeKhoe accommodation to the settlers' society was the order of the day. The pattern of accommodation and sporadic resistance, it seems to us, is well explained by the gradual way in which Europeans infiltrated KhoeKhoe land one spring or spruijt at a time.

text: Abstract: The paper argues that the immigration of single European males to the Cape throughout the Dutch period has been overlooked in the debate about the expansion of the frontier. The presence of these immigrants affected the demography of the settlement and accounts for the consistently high free male sex ratio at the Cape. The paper challenges the mythology of large self-perpetuating pre-1707 settler families using up available land and pushing the frontier forward. It also draws attention to the fact that the Dutch East India Company, while not actively supporting immigration, was favourably disposed to able-bodied single men in their service taking up residence at the Cape as thousands of successful applications for burgher status indicate. These immigrants, drawn from economically depressed urban areas of Northern Europe, cautiously entered the settler economy first as knechts, bywoners, hunters, traders and graziers, before ultimately acquiring their own farms. It was they, who as early as 1702, made contact with the Xhosa. Moreover, they vied with Cape-born men for marital partners. Local women, both slave and free, showed a preference for the newcomers, demonstrating a tendency to exogamy not appreciated in the persistent mythology of a closed settler community, or a herrenvolk democracy.

text: A heated debate still rages around the character of European frontier settlement in early colonial South Africa.  For the purpose of this paper I have chosen a Turnerian definition of the frontier, i.e. the area between the deepest settler penetration and the outer periphery of settlement. An excellent overview of the recent historiography of the frontier is Nigel Penn, "The northern Cape frontier zone in the South African frontier historiography," in Lynette Russell, ed., Colonial Frontiers: Indigenous-European encounters in settler societies (Manchester: Manchester University Press, 2001), 19-46.  * On the one side of this debate, Leonard Guelke, a historical geographer, has recently revived, and refined, the classic interpretation of an earlier generation of historians, such as George McCall Theal, Eric Walker and P.J. Van der Merwe.  George McCall Theal, History of South Africa (Cape Town: C. Struik, 1964 facsimile edition) 11 Vols., 3:474; 3:486; Eric Walker, A History of Southern Africa (London: Longmans, 1968 Impression), 66; 76; P. J. Van der Merwe, Die Trekboer in die Geskiedenis van die Kaapkolonie (Cape Town, Nasionale Pers, 1938).  * Guelke's findings, based on detailed research in the Deeds Office in Cape Town, suggest that frontier movement was the last resort of the descendants of the original (pre-1707) settlers.  Leonard Guelke, "Frontier Settlement in Early Dutch South Africa", Annals of the Association of American Geographers, 66 (March 1976): 25-42; see the commentary on "Frontier Agriculture: Subsistence or Commercial?" by William Norton and Leonard Guelke, Annals of the Association of American Geographers, 67, 3 (September, 1977): 463-467.  * According to this view, the high fertility of the predominantly Dutch and French women led to considerable pressure on the land supply. This “overpopulation” and land shortage forced the younger descendants into the interior. There, these trekboers (=migrant farmers), as they came to be known, struggled in an effort to retain their independence and way of life, even at considerable financial loss.  Guelke, "Frontier Settlement", 39 'in the stock-farming regions everyone remained rather poor'.  * At the risk of caricaturing the complex argumentation of this interpretation, we will refer to this as the ‘diaspora-subsistence’ school.  Eric Walker chose this word as the chapter heading of his chapter four, dealing with South Africa in the years 1717-1778. The word aptly encapsulates the metaphor of the Afrikaner people (volk). The word 'diaspora' implies a dispersion of the 'chosen people' among other nations. The word also underlies the old testament, patriarchal drama and legend of the European race in southern Africa. E. Walker, A History of Southern Africa (London: Longmans, 1968 impression), 76ff.  * On the opposite side of this debate is Solomon D. Neumark, an economic historian, who emphasized the financial opportunities which beckoned from the frontier. While agreeing with the demographic argument, Neumark high-lighted the economic gains to be made by stock-raising and trading with the indigenous people.  Solomon Daniel Neumark, Economic Influences on the South African Frontier, 1652-1836 (Stanford: Stanford University, 1957), 17 and 19.  * For convenience, if not total accuracy, we may refer to this view as the ‘entrepreneurial’ interpretation of frontier expansion in early South Africa. One could also point out that, whereas Guelke emphasized the demographic push behind the frontier, Neumark saw the economic pull of the frontier. The two are not mutually exclusive, but the exact empirical mix remains elusive in the literature.

text: Protagonists in this debate assume that immigration from Europe stopped early in the eighteenth century. Therefore, the demographic pressures underlying expansion must have been the result of natural increase of the original settler population. Coupled with the Roman-Dutch practice of partible inheritance and assumed subdivision of property, this natural increase accounted for the rapidity of frontier penetration and settlement.

Therefore, the demographic pressures underlying expansion must have been the result of natural increase of the original settler population. Coupled with the Roman-Dutch practice of partible inheritance and assumed subdivision of property, this natural increase accounted for the rapidity of frontier penetration and settlement.

text: Guelke and Neumark only disagree about what happened on the frontier: Guelke's frontiersman is best pictured as a depressed Dutch-speaking would-be squire contemplating his solitude, debts and the veld. Neumark's frontiersman, in contrast, is an active, bright-eyed Yankee trader, who with his wagon-load of trinkets, ironware and stock, traverses the tricky terrain of the interior. Both they and many other earlier and modern historians share the belief of the importance of the demographic pressures of the large settler family in creating the pre-conditions for European expansion.  Guelke "Frontier Settlement," 25, where he writes: 'the frontier movement was basically demographic in character'; Richard Elphick, Kraal and Castle (New Haven: Yale University Press), 221; Robert Ross 'at the simplest level, the reason for the expansion of white settlement is quite evident. It lies in the immense population increase of the Afrikaners' in Ross,"The Frontier and the Family: some hypotheses", mimeo 1; and "...the most obvious explanation for the regular breaking up of colonial families was their immense size and the consequent high rate of population growth. It is known, for instance, that in the course of the eighteenth century the free population of the Cape Colony (excluding Khoe-khoe and Busmen) grew at about 2.6 percent per annum, and that was only marginally the result of immigration." In Leonard Thompson and Howard Lamar, eds., The Frontier in History: North America and Southern Africa Compared (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1981), 217 (emphasis added).  *

text: Indeed, the emphasis on large family size of the settlers provides a touchstone for much of the historiography of the contemporary Afrikaner volk: the large family size explains the Afrikaners’ emphasis on family values and codes of behaviour; it explains the Afrikaners’ patriarchal character; it explains the cherished cultural and biological endogamy of the group; it explains the nostalgia of the plaasroman (farm romance), but most importantly, it explains the ensuing population pressure and dramatic dispersion over the continent.  Walker, History, 66; 76.  * In short this demographic explanation lies close to the heart of all attempts to understand the eighteenth-century European South African. Much therefore is at stake in the debate.

text: The first hint that this pervasive interpretation is an inadequate explanation for settler expansion into the interior, is comparative in nature. If historians of South Africa were correct in their demographic explanation of early South African settler expansion, the New England colonies should provide an analogue for the South African case. For, in New England there was a clear immigration watershed date: after 1640, immigration stopped for a century.  Herbert Moller, "Sex Composition and Correlated Culture Patterns of Colonial America", William and Mary Quarterly, 2nd Series, 2 (1945): 125.  *

text: After this date these colonies were dependent on natural increase for demographic growth. The New England area and the Cape colony should then have some demographic features in common after immigration ceased in each respective area. But it is at this point that the demographic comparison becomes difficult to sustain. Whereas the New England colonies did grow by natural increase, reaching near equal sex ratios by 1700, the settler population of the Cape colony never, in the eighteenth century, reached the point where the number of males equalled the number offemales (see figures 1 and 2).  The calculations in figures l and 2 are based on the database PopuCape and Bylaag (H) in Coenraad Beyers, Die Kaapse Patriotte (Cape Town: Juta, 1929), 240-249.  *

One can see the dramatic effect the French families had on the sex ratio after 1688.

text: Although both New England and Cape women undoubtedly did have high fertility rates, the consistently high and imbalanced sex ratios at the Cape especially after the 1720s inform us that some other factor interfered with the gross rate of population growth. The only possible explanation for the high sex ratio is massive and sustained immigration of males throughout the eighteenth century. This is confirmed by thousands of requests for burgher status (the rough equivalent of colonial citizenship) by single male employees of the Dutch East India Company (hereafter DEIC)  Leibbrandt, Requesten, 5 Volumes.  * and by thousands of applications for leningplaatsen (=loan farms) from recently arrived German-speaking immigrants.

text: It is worth pursuing the demographic history of each colonial area, for frontier settlement in both was in lock-step with quite different demographic pressures. New England frontier movement was due to internal demographic pressures, while South African frontier settlement was due, in part, to external, in this case, European economic pressures, leading to emigration to South Africa. To illustrate, by the end of the eighteenth century, the first US federal census of 1790 revealed sex ratios of below 100 for all the older, settled areas of New England.  Moller, "Sex Composition,"125; according to Moller, "a matter of long standing."  * In Woburn, Massachusetts, for instance, the sex ratio had dropped to eighty- seven.  Alexander Keyssar, "Widowhood in Eighteenth-Century Massachusetts: A Problem in the History of the Family," Perspectives in American History 8 (1974): 96.  * What was happening was that the older settled areas, under pressures of land shortage, were becoming distributing centres for restless younger male generations. Young males were leaving to go to the western and northern frontiers. In colonial America, the frontier attracted younger males, while the older, settled areas collected the females. This process continued until at east 1840.  James Edward Davis, Frontier America 1800-1840: a Comparative Demographic Analysis of the Settlement Process (Glendale, California: A.H. Clark Co., 1970).  *

text: A similar process should have occurred in the Cape Colony if frontier settlement there was, as historians claim it to be, due to natural increase. However, as figure one and figure two show, this process—males on the frontier, females in the older settled areas—never occurred in South Africa in the eighteenth century. There were no surplus women in the older areas—the Cape and Stellenbosch districts. Stellenbosch, the second oldest district, founded in 1680, consistently had the highest sex ratios throughout the period 1701-1793. We are far better off if we momentarily jettison the notion that natural increase can—on its own— account for settler expansion and frontier settlement.

text: A comparative perspective from another American colony helps us to understand the process more clearly. The settler population of the Cape Colony much more closely resembles the early seventeenth century male-dominated Virginian population than it does New England. But after the second half of the seventeenth century, mortality of the Virginian indentured male servants inexplicably dropped.  R. Thompson, "Seventeenth-century English and colonial sex ratios: a Postscript", Population Studies 28, 1 (1974): 153-165.  * Consequently, the colony gradually became less and less dependent on European immigration and more dependent on natural increase. By the beginning of the eighteenth century, Virginian natural increase had resulted in near equal sex ratios.  Personal communication with E. S. Morgan; Wesley Frank Craven, White Red and Black: the Seventeenth Century Virginian (Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia, 1971), 26.  * The Cape colony, on the other hand, seemed stuck in a male-dominated pattern, which the Virginian population had begun to escape from twenty-five years after the collapse of the Virginian Company in 1624. The point that we must derive from this comparison, is that during both colony’s respective ‘corporate’ periods, their demographic profiles were almost mirror images of each other. he Cape corporate period was the longest in the  pre-modern colonial world.

Eric Walker's views on immigration are heavily dependent on George McCall Theal. Thea1, History, 3:474; 486.* These became dominant, being repeated in school text books in the twentieth century. For example, Walker wrote that after the settler revolt of 1707:

text: . . . the Seventeen were so alarmed that they decided to send no more immigrants to the Cape. The period of settlement was over and there was no more assisted immigration worth speaking of until the coming of the English Settlers in 1820. Throughout the eighteenth century, immigration was of the slightest; the main additions to the seventeen hundred free burghers men women and children of 1707 were due to natural increase. Hence the importance of the existing handful of Europeans was far greater than their numbers would seem to warrant.   Walker, History, 66.  *

text: Again, according to Walker, 1707 was not the only date after which immigration ‘stopped”. Referring to the 1717 decision to base the Cape Colony on slave labour, Walker would write: “as it was, the work of 1707 was completed in 1717. The colony, denied a steady recruitment of immigrants, was condemned to slave labour.”  Walker, History, 76.  * For English-speaking South Africa, Walker had thereby helped create the myth of a self-contained Afrikaner volk, drawn from the small genetic stock of pre-1707 stamvaders. A national myth was born by the creation of what we will see were quite artificial immigration watershed dates.

text: With reference to the French Refugees who came over here with the intention of learning their living by farming, we assisted them as far as possible to settle down, in accordance with the instructions of the Hon. Company. But there are already many of that kind settled here, some of them ill-behaved, while, more important, they have a limited knowledge of farming, and ....about it, thus causing much poverty among themselves, so that, in the end, they are likely to become burdensome to the Company and the poor fund, especially as at present there are many old people among them who have not many more years to live, and are not able to earn much, if anything at all. So that we would rather, if it please your Excellencies, not to be burdened with such refugees for the future; but would refer to have sent out to us farmers from Zeeland, of an industrious type, who have a thorough knowledge of farming, and who happen to be inclined to make the voyage here in order to improve our farming methods. These would be far more suitable for this country, and would be of much more service and value to the Colony.  Botha, French Refugees, 160.  *

text: Although Mentzel, writing in the late 1780s did not recall the finer points of Bax's views, that he did remember Bax's regulations at all, is important for this implies that they provided the main guidelines through the eighteenth century. Mentzel wrote that under the Governorship of Bax, the Company had given express orders that all soldiers and sailors who desired to leave the Company's service and set up as burghers and carry on private vocations, or to become agricultural or livestock farmers ‘should not be prevented [emphasis added]’.  Mentzel, Description, 1:64.  * Mentzel, our most reliable and certainly the most indefatigable commentator on social life at the Cape in the eighteenth century, nowhere mentions 1707 or 1717 as being watershed dates for immigration. It would be strange if he did, for Mentzel, like 4,000 odd other Germans was an eighteenth century German immigrant himself.  Hoge, "Personalia of the Germans at the Cape 1652-1806" (Cape Town: Archives Year Book, 1946), preface, 1; and see DSAB, s.v. 'Mentzel'.  * Furthermore, nowhere during or after 1707, have I been able to find a specific letter, Resolution, or Plakkaat concerning immigration, which assuredly should have existed. Probably, the Cape letter of 1699 was all that was required to put an end to the short-lived—and therefore anomalous—experiment of assisted familial immigration of the Huguenots.

text: An increase in the European population in this country if such could take place, would be to the Company's advantage and to that of the Colony, as greater trade, an increase in the Company's revenue and an inducement to find new means of subsistence will be the result, especially as the country is large enough to feed and carry a large population . . . Such emigrants should not be encumbered with families, but should be unmarried farm labourers from Europe. They should be sent out from time to time and be placed with well-to-do persons (who have more than they can manage) for a certain number of years at a fixed wage, so that at the expiration of their term of service, their savings and their knowledge of the country and climate would enable them to make a choice of the occupations for which they are best suited.  The Reports of Chavonnes... 103-5; cf. Morgan, American Slavery, 114.  *

Such emigrants should not be encumbered with families, but should be unmarried farm labourers from Europe. They should be sent out from time to time and be placed with well-to-do persons (who have more than they can manage) for a certain number of years at a fixed wage, so that at the expiration of their term of service, their savings and their knowledge of the country and climate would enable them to make a choice of the occupations for which they are best suited.The Reports of Chavonnes... 103-5; cf. Morgan, American Slavery, 114.*

text: Although de Chavonne's picture of the possible course the Cape Colony's economy might follow did not take place, everything in his second paragraph, regarding indentured labour, did. Consider that less than twenty of the immigrants who came to the Cape in the eighteenth century were married when they arrived.  Hoge, "Personalia ...", preface 1 and 488-492 .  * Consider, when we read of Chavonnes’ ‘farm labourers from Europe’ that Mentzel, writing sixty years later, would claim that many of the indentured knechts were ‘European peasant lads’ which surely is an elegant synonym for “unmarried farm labourers.”  Mentzel, Description..., 1:100.  * Consider that requesten to the Council of Policy all follow the form of de Chavonnes’ suggestions. For example, Andries Bester of Maagdenburg, who arrived in the colony in 1712 as a soldier requested in 1721 for burgher papers noting that he had “applied himself to agriculture and believed that he knows enough of it to get his living honestly.”  LR 1 (no 13): 52, s.v. "Bester".  * The best evidence that de Chavonnes suggestions were incorporated is from the quantitative data. True, the DEIC did step up their Cape-based slaving operations to Madagascar, but equally importantly, 1717 to 1795 saw no diminution of foreign-born DEIC sailors and soldiers taking out burgher papers.  LR 1-5, passim; Hoge, "German Personalia," passim.  *

text: Immigration policy concerning European families would briefly arise again in 1750 and 1751. This time the DEIC consulted all the heemraden (magistrates) in the various districts, hoping that they would be able to provide an on-the-spot evaluation of prospective families’ prospects. Heemraden from Stellenbosch and Drakenstein were all agreed that “it was not possible for any additional families to earn a living here.”  The Reports of Chavonnes, 153-155.  * After this date European male immigration continued. text: Immigration policy in the early Cape reveals a clear consistency: there were no sudden breaks; certainly no laws promulgated against European immigrants. From the beginning of the European occupation, the DEIC favoured North European, Protestant males of prime age. Consequently, Dutch, German, Scandinavian, and Swiss bachelor settlers dominated European immigration patterns in the eighteenth century Cape.

text: An analysis of the origins of Cape immigrants confirms that Bax’ policy was not a dead letter. The origins of the immigrants to the Cape reflect a variety of origins over Northern Europe. Few came from obviously rural areas. Instead, with few exceptions the immigrants came from the great urban, industrial and commercial cities in Dutch, German, Scandinavian and Polish areas. In order of numerical importance, the immigrants came from Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Koningsbergen and Hamburg. And without any particular order, Copenhagen, Berne, Maastricht, Delft, Raden (Poland) Cologne, Leipzig, Leiden, Antwerp, Flensburg (Danish Baltic port), Dresden, Danzig and so on. Out of a random sample of 130 immigrants, ninety such cities were represented. Some requesten only provided the area e.g. Hanover, Hessel-Cassel (Duchy), Mecklenburg (Duchy) but the cumulative evidence is compelling. Cape immigrants, like their new world counterparts, came from diverse urban backgrounds, which contradicts Mentzel’s comments regarding “farmlabourers” somewhat.  T. H. Breen and Stephen Forster, "Moving to the New World: The Character of Early Massachusetts Immigration," William and Mary Quarterly, 30 (April, 1973): 193 ff.  *

heading: Estimates of immigration
text: Estimates of immigration

text: Having established that historians of South Africa have unintentionally confused the simplicity and overall consistency of the Cape’s de jure policy and certainly the de facto experience of Cape immigration, we may begin to turn to estimates of the rates of immigration during the eighteenth century. We know that the German immigrants were ninety-nine percent male. J. Hoge’s researches found only forty two legal woman immigrants. Since a naturally increasing population with no immigration—what demographers call a closed population—has near equal sex ratios, we should have a good estimate of the immigrant population if we divide the number of males by the number of females and multiply by 100 which is the demographer’s standard sex ratio. The surplus males must represent the immigrant portion of the community. We have reasonably reliable censuses (the opgaafs) for nearly every year. If these opgaafs err, they err on the side of underestimating the number of males in the distant country districts. The opgaaf also exclude all Company servants and the members of the garrison (nearly all male).  These were separately tabulated in the Monsterrollen.  * These sectors of the population were heavily male-dominated, but we can exclude them from consideration, as we are mainly interested in free settlement and expansion. Furthermore, although there were garrison outposts in the outlying districts, these followed, rather than led, frontier expansion.

text: Figure 1 shows the standardized sex rations of the burgher population for the entire century: they are high, close to Virginian estimates. The Cape sex ratios vary from a high of 600 in the seventeenth century before the arrival of the Huguenots to a low of 117 in 1819. At all times in this period the Cape settler population was dependent on immigration for a large part of its gross rate of increase. We can further refine these figures, for we are not interested in the role that young children (i.e. below fourteen) played in the settler expansion and frontier settlement. The adult sex ratio is even a more precise measure of the immigration process. As can be seen from figure 1, the adult sex ratios were significantly higher. Fluctuations are sharper, reflecting changes in immigration more clearly. The standardized sex ratio is heavily modulated, or dampened, by the equal sex ratios of the large number of colonial children as the settler population creolised.

text: The adult sex ratios confirm that the Cape settler adult society was predominantly male, unlike New England, but similar to Virginia before 1624.

text: In figure 2 we notice that the Cape adult sex ratios show considerable district differentiation. With the exception of Stellenbosch district, the highest ratios prevailed in the areas most distant from the urbanized Cape district. What does this mean? The density of European population varied greatly between districts. The intensive wine and wheat farming areas of the Cape and Stellenbosch districts had the highest densities, according to Guelke, about one free person per square kilometre. Along the high rainfall coastal areas the density decreased to one free person per 10.4 km2. In the interior, the extensive grazier areas, the density was low between one free person per 12.9 km to 25.9 km2.   Guelke, "Frontier Settlement", 34-35.  * The carrying capacity of the land for European settlers was reflected in the size of their farms. The typical grazier's loan farm was 2,500 hectares, while an arable farm i the Western Cape was only fifty one hectares. As one moved from the high rainfall (over twenty inches per annum) areas along the coastal belt, the carrying capacity of the land dropped precipitously.

text: Re-arranging Thomas Malthus’ variables somewhat, we may visualize the process whereby the settler population, growing geometrically by natural increase and immigration, moved into areas which had a geometrically decreasing carrying capacity. Thus, the frontier required far, far fewer people to populate it than (say) the Cape peninsula. The twenty inch rainfall line explains the rapidity of expansion into the interior far more persuasively than does population pressure itself. Frontier settlement at any given time involved only a small fraction of the Cape Colony's European population. The immigrant fraction of the Cape population was never small as we have seen. Hoge, in his exhaustive directory of Germans at the Cape, estimated in his preface that at least 4,000 German immigrants settled at the Cape between 1652 and 1795.  Hoge, "Personalia," preface, no pagination, [page one of two].  * Most of these came in the eighteenth century, their rate of immigration accelerating after 1713 and stabilising after 1750 (see figure 1).

text: In addition to these settlers there was a transient German male population of 10,000 in the same period who did not settle. Of the 4,000 plus Germans who took out burgher papers, only 100, according to Hoge, repatriated. Applications for burgher status in the Requesten (1713-1806) confirm that most immigrants were of German origin, although a handful came from Holland, Portugal, France, etc. A rough calculation, based on page counting of the Requesten suggests that between 1701 and 1793, about 3,500 to 3,800 legal male immigrants took out burgher papers. In 1793 the adult male population, both immigrant and colonial-born, at the Cape was only 4,032. Further elaboration of these estimates awaits intensive research.

text: C. R. Boxer has provided us with a vivid portrait of the conditions in the Netherlands in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.  Boxer, Dutch Seaborne Empire, 55-58.  * Penury, beggary and unemployment existed side by side with obvious prosperity. Foreign vagabonds and disbanded mercenary soldiers mingled with the poor. and economically desperate. A large section of the Dutch working class lived on the brink of poverty and unemployment. To make matters worse, the prosperity of the Netherlands as a whole, drew the unemployed and under-employed from the rural areas of Holland and neighbouring countries. These migrant workers were always willing to take casual work at any price. One obtains the impression from Boxer's essay that the cities of the Netherlands were a scrimmage of all the restless rabble of Europe.  Boxer, Dutch Seaborne Empire, 58; "Sedentary Workers and Seafaring Folk" in Ibid., 54-83.  *

text: It is almost incredible how men try to force their way into the service of the Company. I myself have seen men scramble up to the window of the second story [East India House, Amsterdam] above the entrance door and wait there, hanging on to the iron grating until the door was opened and them immediately let go, fell on the heads of the men standing around the door and in this way got carried in to the house. text: Such desperate economic periods would pass. Accompanying their passing would be such eager, voluntary recruits. Boom times in Europe would lead to impressment and the rise of Zielenverkoopers (literally sellers of souls). These men would enmesh ignorant youths into complex debts and obligations, leading to company service. The character of emigration from Europe then, was cyclical: bad times resulted in voluntary recruitment; boom times resulted in impressment.

text: But we would be mistaken if we thought that this cyclical pattern was directly reflected in immigration to the Cape. The troughs and peaks of the waves of the European economy carrying the emigrants did not break predictably on the shores of the Cape colony. The process was more complicated. The undulating Cape adult sex ratios do not reflect a one-to-one ripple response of the North European economic conditions. Such European economic conditions did influence the decision of the would-be emigrant to leave Europe, but his decision to leave the Company at the Cape and become a burgher immigrant was in turn more closely tied to local Cape economic conditions.

text: Although the Cape, especially the port, was closely tied to the European economy, local agricultural conditions, harvest failures, stock diseases, small-pox etc., all attenuated this relationship. Typically, the would be emigrant would join or be forced to join the company, and would arrive at the Cape. He would then wait and chose the appropriate time to petition the Council of Policy for burgher papers. Such immigrants were using the Company as a temporary bulwark against possible hard times. They preferred the security, but low pay, of the average Company employee to the risky adventure of going it alone in the interior (or anywhere), when local economic conditions were unfavourable. Thus, it is not surprising that Leonard Guelke's attempted correlation of applications, new land in the Cape, with an index of world market conditions—shipping movements around the Cape—did not work.  Charles Randolph Boxer, TheGuelke, "Frontier Settlement", 39-40 and figure 4.  *

text: Statistically, one would say that the two series were co-variants of the economic condition. The graph does not imply that the same people who were applying for burgher status were applying for new land. This might be true, but it is not necessary for the argument.  All we would need would be the names of applicants for land, which are available in the Deeds Office and the Receiver of Land Revenue in the Cape Archives.  * All we are saying here is that frontier expansion occurred under favourable local economic conditions.  Not all would be convinced with the degree of correlation between these variables, but using time series and multiple regression techniques, the third degree polynomial r2 is well over .95. This means over 95% of the variance in the variable Leningsplaatsen applications is "explained" by variations in the variable of burgher applications.  * The same economic conditions favoured applications for burgher status.

The graph does not imply that the same people who were applying for burgher status were applying for new land. This might be true, but it is not necessary for the argument.All we would need would be the names of applicants for land, which are available in the Deeds Office and the Receiver of Land Revenue in the Cape Archives.* All we are saying here is that frontier expansion occurred under favourable local economic conditions.Not all would be convinced with the degree of correlation between these variables, but using time series and multiple regression techniques, the third degree polynomial r2 is well over .95. This means over 95% of the variance in the variable Leningsplaatsen applications is "explained" by variations in the variable of burgher applications.* The same economic conditions favoured applications for burgher status.

text: The length of service in the Company provides further insight into the immigration process and its relationship to local conditions. The average length of service from disembarkation in Cape Town to release from the Company and burgher status was 7.5 years (n=150). The median and mode were 5.5 and 5 respectively. The extreme range of observations (1 to 26 years) explains why the average (or mean) was substantially higher. The mean is a measure of central tendency that is more affected by extreme outliers than the median. The discrepancy between the median and mean provides oblique statistical support for the view that company servants chose their period of release, rather than being subject to a fixed contract period. For instance, indentured servants in Virginia had an almost fixed period of service, their mean, mode and median were closely bunched around seven years. They had no choice.

text: Towards a typology of European immigrants

text: We have established three new points: 1) male immigration to the Cape Colony from Europe was high throughout the eighteenth century 2) frontier settlement was predominantly male and European throughout the same period 3) local economic conditions affected frontier settlement and immigration. We must now establish whether the males who immigrated to the colony were the same who settled the frontier? Or, did these male immigrants also settle in the densely populated areas, thereby displacing some of the older settlers onto the frontier? We can answer these questions by linking names from the Requesten to the appropriate opgaafs. Immigrants who applied for burgher status in the Requesten would appear in ensuing years on the burgher rolls (the opgaaf). The latter give some idea of the geographical location of the immigrant's patterns of settlement. In addition the company records, travellers accounts of the period etc., provide ample material to construct many case histories.

text: For convenience, we have divided the immigrants into four major groups. The first group were the bachelor trader-hunters. They lived on the brink of the DEIC legal system, were men seemingly prone to violence, and were usually unmarried.
html: For convenience, we have divided the immigrants into four major groups. The first group were the bachelor trader-hunters. They lived on the brink of the DEIC legal system, were men seemingly prone to violence, and were usually unmarried.

text: The second group were the graziers who, once released from company service set up stock-farming concerns in outlying areas. Such immigrants might have served their apprenticeship on a rich farmer's outlying leningplaats. If they were lucky enough to find a spouse, she was usually a Khoe-khoe or a slave. There was thus a trend to exogamy among this group.

text: The third group were the bijwoners. Such immigrants on leaving the service, or before, would hire themselves to wealthy farmers as loan, or free, servants.  Moodie, The Record, 1:337 and note 2; see "Introductory note on knechts and free blacks" of this paper, supra.  * They would live on or near the farm of their employer. If such knechts did not succumb to drink—an occupational hazard on the wine farms—they might marry one of the farmer’s daughters, or the farmer's widow.

text: Finally, the last group, were the town artisans. They belonged to no guild system however, and became masters of slaves, rather than of their crafts. But whatever group they belonged to, all immigrants had a rôle in settler expansion at the Cape. Whether they actually opened the early frontier like the trader-hunters, or settled in the arable regions, they contributed in large measure to the demographic and economic pressures leading to the spread of the European settlement.

text: The eighteenth century dawned favourably on the trader immigrant. On the fourteenth  February 1700 the cattle trade and the frontier were thrown open to the ‘freemen’.  Elphick, Kraal and Castle, 224.  * We know that the free settlers were not slow to take advantage of this carte blanche for penetration into the interior. There were two or three trading expeditions in the next couple of years.   H.C.V. Leibbrandt, Precis of the Archives of the Cape of Good Hope, Vol 4: The Defense of Willem Adriaan van der Stel (Cape Town: W. A. Richards, 1897), hereafter Defense, 135.  * One of the best documented expeditions took place in the late summer of 1702. We shall join this expedition, a group of forty-five European men bivouacked at the foot of the Hottentots-Hollands mountain on the morning of the 20th or 21st March, 1702. This symbolically named mountain—first hurdle to the frontier—was sixteen miles from Cape Town. While they are waiting for their colonial-born counterparts to bring them permission from the Governor. We will inspect their camp and supplies. Each adventurer had a Khoe-khoe servant. The fifty odd khoe would serve as guides, porters and handymen in the long eight month expedition.

text: The four wagons were heavily loaded. Almost half a ton of gunpowder and rondscharp (round bullets) had been brought at the recent Kermis (fair) from a colonial-born burgher. We may surmise that this was done to avoid drawing suspicion. The usual course for an individual would be to buy gunpowder from the company stores.  Gunpowder estimates, Defense, 143.  * In one wagon the men had loaded the food stores: rice, brandy and meal were the basic provisions. Thirty-two slaughter oxen scattered among the wagons were the mobile meat supply; they would prove to be an unnecessary extravagance and hindrance. The most important cargo was on the other wagons. In the order of listing these items of trade were: tobacco, dagga (cannabis) ironware, beads and copper. Again, all items were bought from a local burgher. Each trader had contributed twenty-six Rixdollars to the entire undertaking, purchase of stores, hire of wagons and the wages of the Khoe-khoe servants. In addition, a small cavalry was attached: fourteen of the traders had horses. All were armed wth the harquebuses of the day.  An harquebus was in size between a musket and a small cannon, which on account of its weight and recoil was supported on a small trestle. W. W. Greener, The Gun and its Development, 9th ed. (London : Arms and Armour press, 1910), 59.  *

text: The traders were a clannish group yet only one of the forty-five frontier traders, Wynand Wynandz, was born in the colony. Some had military nicknames such as ‘de Haan’ (the hammer of a flintlock, or ‘cock’), ‘Bombam’(lit. bomb blast), Besemboutjie (a small bolt on the stock of a gun, possibly the hook of a gun).  Nicknames: Defense, 138.  * Some post mortem swaggering became evident after the expedition. Otto Samuels from Gröningen in Prussia had witnessed the death of two of his comrades on the trip. The abrupt encounter with death must have reminded the immigrant adventurer of his own possible demise. He drew up his will in the same year. In this document, he specified that he wished “to be carried to his grave by young men, his body being garlanded with flowers and his head garlanded with a crown.”  Hoge, "Personalia", 353; his heir was to be Hans Jacob Konterman, another German; the testament reads "Hem door jongman te laten dragen en zijn doode lichaam gekist zynde te versieren met een kroon op't hoof en met bloemen aan 't lighaam," MOOC 1:41.  * This seems like a reference to his comrades: most of the expedition members were young men although a few were older, in their early forties.

text: Further illustrating the fraternal character of the traders was their covenant. Before disbanding, the traders had all signed a pact, binding themselves to secrecy of the details of the expedition. They wrote their vows in the blank pages of a proto-nationalist Christian book they had on the expedition, Adam Westerman’s De Christelike Zeevaart [The Christian Voyage].  Adam Westerman, Groote Christelijke zee-vaart, in XXVI; predicatien, in maniere van een zeepostille: in welken een schipper koopman oorlogs-volk zee-ende reysende-man geleert wort ende ook andere kan leeren hoe men in de vreese Godes Godtsaligh en voorspoedigh in zijne reyse gelijk ook; verryckt met gebeden enliedekens, ...; met de beschijvingh van Stavoren (Amsterdam: Gysbert de Groot, 1692. There were various editions, the earliest is 1643). No copy of the 580 page book is available in any South African library and only a few are in Dutch libraries, cf. F. W. D. C. A. text: But coming to the Netherlanders, Hollanders, Zeelander, Friese, etc. What shall we say of them, but that they all excel as seafarers, and might well be called Neptune's brood, Tritonic Sea children (so to speak), the makers of all sorts of ships, who yield to no nation in the world in quick and adroit navigation, skilful, and who carry on massive trade and wage mighty war at sea with very little help, roaming around the world and opening up every corner they have seen so far; and through the Most High's blessing their domain has become like a map of the whole earth, and like a sea into which all rivers of the earth's goods discharge: a land swarming with all kinds of peoples, a Land of Milk and Honey, a widely renowned Tyre, a learned Athens, an inn for the Church of God, a wonder of the world, a scourge to Spain and the Indies, a land which is devoted to God, an Island encircled by water as with arms, so full of convenient harbors, ports and roads, that one might well say:

text: And where all other Lands, Like Egypt, Libya, Persia, Ethiopia, etc., are heavily plagued by savage animals, crocodiles, lions, bears, leopards, tigers,wolves, etc., vipers, serpents, scorpions, etc., our land is free of these. Also in our country it is not too hot, like in Guinea and Sao Tome; nor too cold, like in Novaya Zemlia and Spitsbergen. Our shortest day has just 7.8 hours of sunshine, the longest day 17.17 hours. Where is there a province so blessed, so prosperous?  As quoted in Allison Blakely, Blacks in the Dutch World: The Evolution of Racial Imagery in a Modern Society (Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1993), 1; see also Defense, 142.  *

text: After waiting for three days, the traders were rewarded with the sight of Jacob van der Heyden and Ferdinand Appel. These two burghers claimed they brought the Governor's permission—denied by the Governor  Defense, 133. "Without giving the least notice of their intention"  * and, also blessings from a higher authority. “Proceed now in the name of God” was the burghers’ valediction. Their small task completed, Van der Heyden and Appel then turned their horses and headed towards the comforts of their family life in nearby Stellenbosch.  Defense, 137.  * The expedition began quietly enough. Trade, albeit perfunctory, was quite regularly conducted. After a month's journey into the interior the traders paid Captain Koopman (a Khoe chieftain) some tobacco for ten cattle and forty sheep. Later, at the Gamtoos River, the traders obtained one calf and three sheep, again paying with tobacco, keeping the dagga for the Xhosa-speaking farmers on the frontier.  Richard Elphick informs us that the Xhosa probably were probably 'uninitiated' in 1702; Jeffrey Peires points out there are references to Xhosa supplying dagga to Khoe khoe and San (e.g. Queen Hoho of the Amathole mountains). The usual Xhosa words for dagga are umya and usango, i.e. not loan words, which would suggest there was an autochthonous usage, cf. Andrew Smith, "Contribution to South African Materia Medica" (3rd Edition, Lovedale: 1895), 20, where he writes that although dagga is used extensively in folk cures for snakebite, horse sickness, it is red dagga (rooibaard or, Leonotis leonurus or klip dagga, Leonotis ovata ) not the usual green dagga. Personal communications with the author.  *

text: But the further they travelled from the settlement at de Kaap, the rate of exchange of the traders not only dropped, but the mode of exchange changed. ‘Soetekoek', one of the accompanying Khoe servants, confirmed this when he gave the following testimony to the DEIC investigation which ensued: “The Dutch first came during the night at the kraal of Karmon, [which was surrounded by bushes]. They [the ‘Dutch’] kept quiet until daylight and then fired into the kraal. The natives took to flight and left their cattle behind..”.  Defense, 137.  *

text: This was a dress-rehearsal for a series of such raids. A pattern had emerged: during the night the raiders kept quiet until daybreak when they surrounded and attacked the kraals, shooting into them. The khoe-khoe, with their wives and children did their best to escape, but the Dutch pursued the fleeing Khoe and fired after them and obtained possession of all their cattle, which they took from the kraals. The Khoe auxiliaries witnesses did not have an accurate estimate of the stock captured, but all agreed the ‘troops were very big’.  Defense, 137.  *

text: Once the party came into contact with the Xhosa, the raiders adopted the same techniques they had used against their Khoe-khoe neighbours. However, some friendly Khoe-khoe had apprized the Xhosa of the European incursion. Consequently, the Xhosa had risen to meet these latter-day Teutonic knights. While the Xhosa were now on a war footing, they were still taken by surprise by the tactics of the dawn raiders. Once again the raiders surrounded the unsuspecting sleeping camp. Once again they must have silently erected the trestles for their harquebuses on the rim of the camp. The primitive weapons worked most efficiently at close range.  Defense, 137-8.  *

text: The Khoe witnesses could not form an estimate of the dead Xhosa, except that the number ‘must have been rather large.’ One Khoe witness ‘found twenty dead and afterwards at different spots, two, three and more together.’  Defense, 138.  * Two features of this raid distinguishes it from the Khoe raids: first, much greater brutality of the Europeans was in evidence. The same Khoe witness related that ‘the captured kaffers, had by order of the Dutch, been beaten to death with sticks by the Hottentots of Captain Snel.’  Defense, 137-138.  * The second distinguishing feature was resistance. Despite the surprise attack, the raiders found one of their number squatting on his haunches with an assegai sticking through his torso. Another member died of ‘natural causes.’ Khoe witnesses further related that the Xhosa had sworn vengeance and were preparing to attack the colony.  Defense, 138 ff.  *

text: The return of the raiding party was slow, because of the thousands of cattle and sheep they had seized. Nearing the settlement, they divided up the spoils and exchanged vows of secrecy and signed their secret covenant in the 600 page book of Adam Westerman. There the matter would have rested, with no one the wiser had not the raiders, as Willem Adriaan Van der Stel put it, spent ‘their booty in great dissipation’.  Defense, 133-4.  * After ‘ripe deliberation’ the DEIC decided to close the frontier trade and investigate the entire affair. From the ensuing enquiry, we learn that this raid was neither the first, nor the only such undertaking.  Defense, 133 and 135; why this expedition has not attracted greater historical enquiry is a mystery. The first reference in the secondary literature would appear to be in J. W. Lancelot Stock's posthumous article "The diary of a cattle expedition among the Hottentots in 1707", English Historical Review 124 (October 1916): 613. John Milton gives a brief account of the expedition in The edges of war: a history of frontier wars 1702-1878 (Cape Town: Juta, 1983), 7-9. Christopher Saunders refers to it in the time-line in his Historical Dictionary of South Africa (Metuchen, New Jersey and London: Scarecrow Press, 1983), xiv; E.C. Godée-Molsbergen, has no mention, see his Reizen in Zuid-Afrika in de Hollandse Tijd. 4 volumes. ('s-Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff, 1916).  *

text: The violent raid was not only the first contact between the European colonists and Xhosa-speaking people, but as we have suggested an important aspect was the character and origins of the immigrant fraternity who conducted the expedition. These young men were certainly not displaced younger sons of the colonial born squirearchy. Wynand Wynandz, the only colonial-born European, was ostensibly in charge of the provisions, but once the expedition was under way, all agreed that he abrogated even this small responsibility. His military rôle in the expedition was that of quartermaster. He probably helped obtain the supplies at the best prices and in secrecy. Once this preparatory work was done, he assumed a back seat in the ensuing expedition, but was among the ringleaders interrogated by the DEIC officials.  Defense, 146-7.  *

text: Bartholomas Nachtigal, born in Danzig, obtained burgher status in 1690. He was renowned for his illegal activities in the colony. A Court of Justice official had earlier commented that he was accustomed to crossing the country with only his blunderbuss, powder and lead; that he was a ‘vagabond’ without any fixed address. A brutal man, Nachtigal had earlier been imprisoned for two years for battering a DEIC field guard. After the expedition Nachtigal went to live in a remote district of Drakenstein. Just before his death he exchanged his flock of 300 sheep for a ‘decent burial’.  Hoge, "Personalia", 290.  *

text: We have too little information to flush out their biographies further. The well indexed Resolutions provide frustratingly little. Few raiders were burghers before the raid. Few were married. That some of the raiders did take out burgher papers during the year of the raid is striking. Was this contrition, or were they illegal types whom the DEIC had finally exposed because of the raid? A slap on the wrist was all that the Cape officials attempted, no doubt, for fear of the reaction of the burghers who had shown considerable sympathy during the interrogations. No one was punished. This, at any rate was the version of Governor William Adriaan van der Stel in his defense, or Korte Deductie.

text: The burghers whose merchant rôle in the expedition was clearly established, indignantly claimed that the adventurers should have been punished. The burghers asserted that the marauders ‘were miscreants, without families and homes, chiefly fugitives from justice and men of loose character who had been imprudently discharged from the Company's service’. Interestingly enough the burghers maintained that the ‘real’ reason why the raiders had not been prosecuted was ‘that the Governor's agents had obtained cattle for him in the same manner, which would be brought to light at a trial.’  Theal, History, 3:416-417 and ff.  *

text: But this evidence was only led at the height of the settler revolt of 1707. Tempers were frayed. Accusations from both the Governor and his supporters and the rebellious burghers filled the air. We know that the raiders believed the Governor gave his permission for the expedition; we also know that some burghers provided provisions. Ferdinand Appel and Jacobus Heyden, who had ridden out to the base camp, were certainly not supporters of the Governor, both were rebels against the Governor in 1707 and were deported to Holland after the settler revolt of 1707. Be that as it may, we do have a clear picture of the raiding group. Male, unmarried, Teutonic, vagabondish and violent, these immigrants provided a spectacular curtain-raiser for the rôle of later immigrants on the hectic stage of the eighteenth-century Cape interior. But what is to make of their proto-nationalist covenant and the hefty volume they carted into the interior? Why was there no punishment? All we may conclude is that it was the Cawlkskys of ths world rather than the Van der Merwes who opened up the frontier in this early period.

text: Despite DEIC trade restrictions in the interior after 1703, such immigrant traders did not disappear. One case history in particular seems typical. Hermanus Lucas Crouse (Krause) arrived in 1755 from Germany as a ship's boy in a DEIC vessel. He took out burgher rights in 1758.  Hoge, "Personalia", 219.  * Invariably absent from the burgher militia, he drew the irate attention of the Stellenbosch officials. When approached by the authorities about his absence, he replied contemptuously ‘Oh, that is nothing after all’. Such insolence led to an enquiry. From this enquiry we may infer that he was engaged in illicit trading and smuggling on the frontier. The officials pointed out that he had sold three hundred cattle at the Salt River market in Cape Town, but only entered sixteen cattle on the yearly opgaaf return.  Moodie, The Record, 3:21-24.  * This discrepancy led to further investigations which revealed a partner, Arnoldus Herring. His origins are obscure, but we do know he was also an ex-DEIC sailor.  Moodie, The Record, 3:34-35.  * Both had travelled to the interior, ‘to the bushes and lurking laces of the Kafirs where they bartered with the Xhosa for cattle, providing beads, iron and copper”.  Moodie, The Record, 3:34-5.  * Although we have no evidence of violence, except an oblique reference to ‘irregularities committed’ which could mean anything, these two traders do not differ in any important way from their 1702 counterparts. Unmarried, of German descent, and operating on the borders of legality, they were following a pattern. Krause eventually applied for and was granted loan farms in the 1770s: another first generation German immigrant was on the frontier.  CAD RLR 21( 1772-1778): passim.  *

text: Even the sceptical Leonard Guelke cedes that the elephant hunter could expect to reap profits from small investments. Both P.J. Van der Merwe and Richard Elphick agree that hunting and trading were intimately linked.  Elphick, Kraal and Castle, 223-4.  * Profits from hunting could be reinvested in trade items. The hunter, knowing the trails, used his knowledge for later trading. Sometimes the trading expedition would turn into a hunting one and vice versa. Such a hunter-trader was George Friederich Rautenbauch. On 17 January 1778 he and some colonial-born burghers ‘rode far into the interior to shoot elephants’. The hunting party proceeded northwards to ‘the great river’(the Orange River?) However, they changed their minds and went ‘South [east ward’ into ‘Kaffirland’. There, each member of the party bartered cattle for himself with the Xhosa. Despite setting out on an elephant-hunt they all had items of trade at hand. For each head of cattle, ‘four bunches of beads and two copper plates’ were exchanged; for each calf, ‘a string of beads.’  Hoge, "Personalia", 326; Moodie, The Record, 3:73-74.  *

text: George Frederich Rautenbauch was born in Frebnitz in Saxon and arrived at the Cape as a soldier in 1757. He applied for burgher status in 1761. Unlike the other professional hunters, he married (in 1762). His spouse, Maria Magdalena Ferreira, like many immigrants’ wives was a widow.  Hoge, "Personalia" , 326; cf. 139ff .  * Rautenbauch applied for a loan farm in 1778,  CAD RLR 20 (1778): 57  * the same year the Lutheran faith was allowed in South Africa. Rautenbauch might have written to his brother about his marital good fortune, outdoor adventures, new farm and the new religious dispensation  in southern Africa. For in 1780 Johan Christoffel Rautenbauch arrived at the Cape. In the same year, the company, now an active agent in the immigration process, conveniently ‘loaned’ Johan Christoffel to his brother. Two years later the newly arrived German immigrant had also married.  Hoge, "Personalia", 326 and following entry.  * Demographers term such processes ‘immigrant chains’, whereby certain members of families act as path-finders in new areas, write to and invite the more timid relatives to leave the ‘old’ country Such ‘immigrant chains’ were much part of the immigration process in eighteenth century South Africa, as indeed they were in America.  Davis, Frontier Demography, passim.  *

text: Mentzel informs us that there were ‘many’ elephant hunters at the Cape.  Mentzel, Biography of Alleman, 96.  * Elephant hunting had become so ingrained as part of the frontier way of life that no young girl would even look at a young fellow who had not been, at least once, op togt (on a hunt). Repeated plakkaats regulating the ivory trade throughout the eighteenth century confirm the widespread nature of the profession.  Plakkaat Boeken, 2-5, passim, indexes. As early as 1735 there were no wild animals west of Cape Agulhas, Mentzel, Description, 1:61.  * Hunters would disappear for six months at a time. ‘Ordinarily’ wrote Mentzel, ‘elephant hunters go out in parties of from fifteen to twenty men. They would penetrate far in advance of the cattle and sheep farmers. Some would reach as far east as Pondoland, and possibly, Natal’.  Walker, History, 91.  * Such hunting was profitable. Abbé de La Caille wrote of three brothers who had achieved every immigrant's dream of making a big enough fortune from big game to return to the fatherland.  Abbé de La Caille, Journal historique. . . (Paris: 1763), 110.  * The hunters did not confine themselves to elephant, but also, pace Mentzel, ‘lions, tigers, rhinoceri, buffaloes, stags, deer, in short, everything that came thei way’.  Mentzel, Biography of Alleman, 95.  *

text: Such an institutionalized life-style understandably produced by-products of violence. For example to these hunters, must be attributed the widespread adoption of the sjambok, a heavy short whip made from rhinoceros hide used for disciplining livestock— and sometimes slaves—in the Western Cape. In 2005, the sjambok is made from plastic and may be purchased at any busy traffic intersection. According to Mentzel, hunters could expect to cut a hundred sjamboks from a single hide. They would sell the individual sjamboks for twenty stuivers each.  Mentzel, Biography of Alleman, 95.  * Violence on the frontier was thereby indirectly exported back to the settled areas where the nautical “cat” had been in use.

text: Anyone who believes that company artisans, once released from their service, humbly plied their trades in Cape Town should look at the case of ‘hunter-immigrant’ Frans Hendrik Marx.  The most famous member of this German family who came to to South Africa was Louise Marx, sister of the famous Karl; she married Jan Carel Juta in Cape Town in 1853 and reared an impressive family of intellectuals and a member of the Cape parliament, Sir Henry Hubert. See J.A. Heese and R.T.J. Lombard, South African Genealogies, 4: 198; Franz Mehring, Karl Marx, The Story of his Life (Ann Arbor: Michigan Press, 1962), 2.  * He arrived at the Cape as a company servant in 1721. Unlike most of the immigrants, Marx came from a small village, of ‘Minden-aan-de-roer’ near Holzweiler Erklenz in Gulik. He asked for burgher papers in the same year claiming that he was ‘a mason by trade’.  LR, 2:744.  * After this period of service, Marx moved to the frontier and set up a small-holding in Mossel Bay. From there (300 miles from Cape Town), he conducted hunting expeditions into the frontier regions until he died in 1791. He was a famous personality throughout the colony. Both Peter Thunberg and Anders Sparrman enjoyed his hospitality.  Sparrman, Travels, 1:95; Hoge, "Personalia", 260.  * Possibly they learnt much from him of frontier conditions, which information they would need for their botanical investigations. Marx was fortunate in finding a spouse, but like many frontiersmen carelessly did not bother to legitimiz the union. Consequently, his only son was illegitimate.  Hoge, "Personalia", 260.  *

text: In the seventeenth century all hunters had to apply for hunting licenses, the records now carefully preserved in the Receiver of Land Revenue Records. These were quite detailed requests indicating where and what the hunter expected to get, e.g. Jan Harmenz van Paderhorn Germany wanted to hunt “omtrent het Riebeeck’s Casteel, een vragt Elands, Hartebeests of Remoter Vleesch,”  CAD RLR, 1 (1700) : 118.  * Some hunters were women. Hunting was part of the early Cape cultural life and had a marked seasonal profile.

text: Of course, not all hunter-traders were immigrants. We are only interested in drawing attention to the rôle of immigrants in such occupations. Opening up the frontier whether by trade or the hunt was not the exclusive province of the young sons of Euro-Cape families. Immigrants from the German-speaking world were also involved in such activities. But then the Germans had strong traditions of such life-styles.

text: Two types of knecht existed at the Cape. The first was a ‘free servant', a sailor or soldier who had been discharged from service, who then hired his own labour at a negotiable wage. Otto Mentzel was such a ‘professional’ knecht. As Anna Boëseken has shown, free blacks also sometimes hired themselves as professional knechts.  Anna Jacoba Boëseken, Slaves and Free Blacks (Cape Town: Tafelberg, 1978), 87-88.  * Knechthood for such people never culminated in burgher status, although free blacks were allowed to purchase land. In the seventeenth-century free blacks did participate in a sort of forced ‘frontier’ expansion. The Heeren XVII had decided that a separate ‘reserve’ should be set aside for free blacks in Stellenbosch. We know from Leonard Guelke's map of the South Western Cape, 1657 to 1757, that this area was present day Jonkershoek. But for some unexplained reason this proto-apartheid movement, engineered in Amsterdam, failed. By 1700, with two exceptions, Rangton of Bali and Jan van Ceylon, the free blacks had returned to Cape Town. There they would stay, preferring the urban life tothe frontier. Davis’ work on the nineteenth century frontier in America reveals that in that different period, blacks did not participate in the frontier expansion either.  Davis, Frontier Demography, passim.  *
html: Two types of knecht existed at the Cape. The first was a ‘free servant', a sailor or soldier who had been discharged from service, who then hired his own labour at a negotiable wage. Otto Mentzel was such a ‘professional’ knecht. As Anna Boëseken has shown, free blacks also sometimes hired themselves as professional knechts.Anna Jacoba Boëseken, Slaves and Free Blacks (Cape Town: Tafelberg, 1978), 87-88.* Knechthood for such people never culminated in burgher status, although free blacks were allowed to purchase land. In the seventeenth-century free blacks did participate in a sort of forced ‘frontier’ expansion. The Heeren XVII had decided that a separate ‘reserve’ should be set aside for free blacks in Stellenbosch. We know from Leonard Guelke's map of the South Western Cape, 1657 to 1757, that this area was present day Jonkershoek. But for some unexplained reason this proto-apartheid movement, engineered in Amsterdam, failed. By 1700, with two exceptions, Rangton of Bali and Jan van Ceylon, the free blacks had returned to Cape Town. There they would stay, preferring the urban life tothe frontier. Davis’ work on the nineteenth century frontier in America reveals that in that different period, blacks did not participate in the frontier expansion either.Davis, Frontier Demography, passim.*

text: The second type was a loaned knecht. These knechts were undischarged servants of the DEIC, in Moodie’s words ‘a class from whom the European knechts were almost exclusively supplied.’  Moodie, The Record, 1:337 and note 2.  * The small number of knechts in the annual opgaafs is misleading. Since knechts were employed for one-year secondments, they had a shorter ‘census life’ than the burghers. Whereas the same free burgher's name would appear on the opgaaf for his natural life, a knecht would appear only once, and then as an integer on the return of the burgher householder. Consequently the annual opgaaf does not allow us to trace the knecht's career trajectory satisfactorily. We can see this process clearly in a rare compilation of figures by H.C.V. Leibbrandt.  Defense, 125.  * According to his list, the annual aggregate of knechts hovered around forty-five. But each year the forty-five knechts were replaced by a further ±forty-five new recruits. Thus, the total number of knechts at the Cape was much higher than one might suspect.

text: Knecht-hood then, was the buffer stage between the company service and full burgher status for nearly all immigrants in the eighteenth century. The grazier immigrant Jurrian Adelar, born in Dresden, arrived in 1705 as a sailor. Between 1705 and 1713 he was loaned as a company knecht to various farmers. In 1713 he was mentioned as a ‘free farmer’ on the farm Helena Bay on the Berg River, on the northern frontier of the settlement. However, he was not yet a burgher. During his service as a farm hand he must have attained the necessary agricultural skills. But the economic dislocation of the colony following poor harvests and the small pox epidemic of 1713 must have been so severe that he waited until 1724 before formally applying for burgher status. In his memorial he wrote that ‘he believes that he will be able to support himself as an agriculturalist’.  Hoge, "Personalia," 2; LR, 1:2.  *  Hoge, "Personalia," 2; LR, 1:2.    In 1731 Jurrian Adelaar appears on the annual opgaaf in the Drakenstein district. In that year he owned two male slaves, one horse, twelve oxen and 300 shep. Apart from the slaves—perhaps they were old shepherds—his holding was typical of the grazier immigrant, i.e., he planted no vines, no barley, no Sicilian corn and no wheat.  Opgaaf, 1731.  *

text: Barend Buijs of Bronswijk was another such immigrant who went to the outlying districts as a grazier. He arrived in 1715 as a soldier and ‘applied himself to agriculture in which he has so well succeeded’ that he petitioned for burgher rights in 1721.  LR 1:51; Opgaaf, 1723; other examples: Johan Christoffel Bek: LR 1:59 and Jan Lodewyk Bower, LR, 1:64, Opgaaf, 1752.  * Two years later, he appeared on the Drakenstein district opgaaf, with twenty oxen and 200 sheep.  Opgaaf, 1723.  * In 1727 he applied for a loan farm.  CAD. RLR 7(1727): 7.  *  Some of these immigrants undoubtedly did not fare well. Andries Bester, an ex-soldier had also ‘applied himself to agriculture’, and believed that he knew ‘enough to it to get his living honestly'. After two years as a burgher of the Drakenstein, all he owned was a weapon. There are no clues as to what his living was.  Opgaaf, 1723.  * Like Adelaar and Buijs, Bester was unmarried.

Sexual frustration provided the main currents of conversation when Anders Sparrman visited a Hanoverian knecht on a remote farm near Paarl in 1774:

text: I arrived in the evening at a farm house, the bailiff of which, a Hanoverian, welcomed me in a most friendly manner with a hearty slap of the hand. He entertained me with milk and an account of the love affairs and intrigues he had when he was a soldier in England . . . He also gave me a list (which by his desire, I took down in my pocketbook, as the result of his own experience) of the constant order of precedence in love which ought to be observed among the fair sex in Africa. This was as follows. First, the Madagascar women, who are the blackest and best; next to these the Malabars, then the Buganese, or Malays, after this the Hottentots and last and worst of all, the European Dutch woman.  Morgan, American Slavery, 236; Sparrman, Travels 1:101.  *

text: Some impatient immigrants did not wait for fortune or destiny to provide a spouse. Such immigrant knechts, bought, manumitted and married their slaves. Johan Paul Gottfried Fabricius, for example, arrived at the Cape in 1766.  LR, 2:457.  * Until 1783, he worked for the Company at a soldier’s pay. After he applied for his burgher papers he worked in the Company hospital as a handyman. At some point he had bought a slave, ‘Rosina of the Cape’, whom he had baptised in 1783 and manumitted two years after he obtained his burgher papers.  LR 2: (no. 155 of 1783): 457.  * He must have married her soon thereafter, for all five children of the union were baptised in the Lutheran Church, established in 1778.  Hoge, "Personalia", 93-94.  * One may conclude that immigration was a three step process for Europeans: first, one came to the Cape, then waited until the conditions were favourable, and only finally, applied for burgher papers.

text: The sex ratios in figure 2 suggest that the preferred area for immigrants was in the district of Stellenbosch. Perhaps a partial explanation for the attractions of this district was that the opportunities, or promise of a spouse were greatest here. Mentzel remarked that knechts ‘frequently married their master's daughter or widow’. He added ‘in fact, I have known cases where widows engaged knechte with a view tdeic matrimony.  Mentzel, Description, 1:164-5.  * All the examples of such liaisons occurred in the Stellenbosch district. We have termed such immigrants bijwoners more from an attempt to distinguish them from the preceding type of grazier knecht, who was in charge of a distant leningplaatsen, than from any positive proof that these knechts actually lived close to the main farmhouse of their master.

text: No better example of an immigrant marrying a widow can be found than Martin Melck, who was also the most materially successful of the eighteenth-century German immigrants. Melck was born in Memmel in Prussia, the son of a boatman. At eighteen, he succeeded in apprenticing himself to the Mason's guild in Riga. Three years later he abruptly joined the DEIC as a soldier. Although he had completed his apprenticeship, he was probably unable to find a suitable position. After a brief spell in the garrison at the Cape, Melck was loaned to a farmer, Johan Phillip Giebeler.

text: After this agricultural stint, Melck tried his hand at mining but this stab at quick wealth (at the Simonsberg mine) only lasted a month. His masonic background and knowledge helped him found a lime and bricks work in Stellenbosch. He supplied the Company with products from this concern on a regular basis.  Hoge, "Personalia", s.v. Hoge, "Personalia", 265-266.  * Suddenly, Martin Melck of Memmel was a rich man. He used his wealth and applied on many occasions for loan farms. In the 1770s, Admiral John Stavorinus visited Melck's farm, or rather plantation, its extent was huge:

text: About four o'clock in the afternoon, we came to the farm of Melck which at a distance, and indeed close by, appeared like a whole village. It lies among the mountains, upon the gentle declivity of a high ridge, and on the banks of an ever-running stream, which he has led along his farm, between two brick walls, like a canal, and which turns a watermill, for the purpose of grinding his corn. His dwelling house, which was of considerable size, had four or five large and handsome rooms, all furnished in a neat, and even costly style, so that it more resembles a gentleman's villa than the mansion of a farmer... Between these warehouses. he had a black smiths’ and carpenters’ workshop, and a cartwright's manufactory, together with other workpeople necessary for so large and troublesome a concern. But few of them were Europeans, the largest number were oriental slaves who had cost him a great deal of money....... A little higher up...stood a range of...buildings, calculated for the slaves, of whom he had full two hundred. For he declared to me that he did not know the exact number.  John Splinter Stavorinus, Voyage to the East Indies (London: C. Y. and G. Robinson) translated Samuel Hull Wilcoke, 3 Volumes, 1:61 ff.  *

text: Melck never learned to read or write or even count. Yet by 1776 he was the owner of ten arable farms, two leasehold farms and three store houses in Cape Town. In one of these warehouses in Cape Town Melck conducted secret Lutheran meetings. The DEIC explained that his request for a Lutheran pastor was untimely.  LR 2: s.v. Lutheran Church; Hoge, "Personalia", 265-266.  * Melck, like many Germans at the Cape, never really assimilated into the reformed tradition. Over the mantel piece on his farm “Elsenburg”, a Prussian eagle presided over the coat of arms of the Prussian monarchy—it is still there. Stavorinus elaborated: “he decorated the chimney pieces, and other parts of his house with the arms of his sovereign, and cherished a fond attachment to his person.”  Stavorinus, Voyage, 1: 66-67.  *

text: In 1776 Melck's wife died. In that year he owned 203 slaves, 170 horses, 1321 cattle, 4,1167 sheep, 106 pigs and 200,000 vines. An immigrant, he was one of the richest men at the Cape. Jan Blignault of Amsterdam was another such immigrant who married well. He arrived in 1723 as an ensign in the service of the DEIC. Three years later he petitioned the Council of Policy for burgher status, modestly pointing out that ‘by his marriage here, he has come into possession of some lands, on which he thinks he can support himself'.  LR, 1:60.  * He married Anna Roussouw, a widow. Anna Roussouw was a descendant of the original well-established stamvader families. ‘Some lands’ in 1732 supported seven horses, 135 oxen, 550 oxen, 37,000 vines and a large corn acreage.  Opgaaf, 1732.  * Every time an immigrant made such a match, a colonial born male was displaced in the elite matrimonial pool. This process, multiplied led to population pressure, but a different kind of population pressure than that espoused by proponents of the ‘diaspora’ school. Itseems clear that colonial born women had clear ideas about the men they preferred. Mentzel would write emphatically: ‘I might add that every girl without exception prefers as her husband a man who has been born in Europe to one who is of colonial birth'.  Mentzel, Description, 2:114.  * Later, Mentzel teased some of the colonial-born daughters by saying that there are so many girls and so few men in the country. The daughters replied in chorus: ‘Oh! that is no trouble, the suitors come from the fatherland (Europe) and therefore no spinsters will be left over.’  Mentzel, Description, 3:104.  * This predilection of the young settler women for foreign suitors was no passing whim. The gallant Paravicini di Capelli, aide de campe to Governor de Mist, was struck by the attentions of the Afrikaner daughters. Accompanying the Governor on a colony-wide tour in 1803, all Paravicini could do was to record his regrets of their all too short visits in his journal. The attentions of one charming daughter on one farm, were followed by the ministrations and coquetry of the next farme's daughter. In one instance, Paravicini after leaving one farm chose to eat a second midday meal, rather than risk offending Pieter Terblanche's ‘two pretty angel-faced daughters’. These daughters both insisted on piling his plate with more food than even the generous codes of the Afrikaner laid down as proper.  W. B. E. Paravicini di Capelli, Journeys in the Interior of South Africa (Cape Town: Van Riebeeck Society, 1965) 226, 228, 231 (two mentions) and 232.  * Although Paravicini modestly reflected that his epaulettes probably were his main attraction, much more than such superficial items were at stake. What Paravicini was experiencing was some healthy exogamic traits of the settler women. This tradition is quite at variance with the ‘diaspora’ school version or the strict biological endogamy of the volk.
