text: Edwardus Christian Houtman (contemporary Haumann) of Riga, demonstrated the pattern of colonial women preferring foreign-born suitors no less than four times in his life. He arrived in 1745 as a Company soldier. Crimps and Zielenverkoopers had kidnapped him in Holland. Once he had overcome the trauma of his abduction, his progress in the marital stakes was rapid. A year after his arrival he had obtained burgher papers.  LR, 2:530.  * In 1749 he was married to Susanne Taillefer, one of the descendants of the French Huguenots. Three years later he married into another old settler family, the Marais clan.  Sparrman, Travels, 1:99 and note 276.  * One year before this marriage he appeared in the Drakenstein opgaaf owning four male and two female slaves, 200 sheep 12,000 vines.  Opgaaf, 1751.  * In 1761 he would marry again, this time into the ubiquitous Roussouw dynasty. His last match was to a young woman, Helena Catharina Krugel, who would outlive him by forty years. H applied for a loan farm in 1780.  CAD RLR 19 (1780): 199.  * Having worked his way through four established colonial families, his hodings were considerable when he died in 1782. In that year his young widow was listed as owning twenty males slaves, five female slaves, five slave children, 100,000 vines, 300 sheep and a large corn farm. She also possessed his new  leningplaats on the frontier, 650 miles from Simondium, another widow on the frontier.  Sparrman, Travels, 1:99  *

text: We have an excellent portrait of Houman, as Anders Sparrman struck up a relationship with him when the botanist visited him on his remote farm near Paarl in 1775. Despite his education as a surgeon in Riga, Houman appears as a poseur anxious to impress Sparrman with his own intellectual prowess. Apparently his continental education had first gained Houman entré into the Taillifer household. We know that it was from Susanne Taillifer, who was ‘a parson's daughter’, that he had obtained his library. Did the elan of a continental education account for the undoubted success of the immigrants incursions into the established families of the embryonic volk? It would seem so. The settlers’ cultural world was framed by the isolation of the frontier. Did this render the European women vulnerable to the attentions of any European man who professed any learning at all, leitmotif of The Story of an Africa Farm? The immigrants certainly brought no wealth with them, which might have acted as an attraction.
html: We have an excellent portrait of Houman, as Anders Sparrman struck up a relationship with him when the botanist visited him on his remote farm near Paarl in 1775. Despite his education as a surgeon in Riga, Houman appears as a poseur anxious to impress Sparrman with his own intellectual prowess. Apparently his continental education had first gained Houman entré into the Taillifer household. We know that it was from Susanne Taillifer, who was ‘a parson's daughter’, that he had obtained his library. Did the elan of a continental education account for the undoubted success of the immigrants incursions into the established families of the embryonic volk? It would seem so. The settlers’ cultural world was framed by the isolation of the frontier. Did this render the European women vulnerable to the attentions of any European man who professed any learning at all, leitmotif of The Story of an Africa Farm? The immigrants certainly brought no wealth with them, which might have acted as an attraction.

text: If Martin Melck and Edward Houman were the Horatio Algers of South Africa, we must not be misled into believing that their material prosperity and impressive mobility were in any way typical. Being wealthy, their biographies are naturally full. Nor should we believe Mentzel's solipsistic wishful thinking that knechts ‘usually make their fortune at the Cape’.  Mentzel, Description, 2:101.  * The opgaafs throughout the eighteenth century tell quite a different story. Between a third and a half of all burghers were without land, often without even a horse, and in desperate cases, without even guns. Because of their poverty, these ‘poor whites’ left few traces in the records. To reconstruct their lives is time-consuming. Three case histories demonstrate their plight.

text: Paulus Albregt of Pifhchen, Breitungen, arrived at the Cape in 1744 as a company sailor.  LR, 1: 6.  * Five years later he asked for burgher papers. In 1752 he appeared in the Drakenstein district without any property. Thirty years later he had retreated to the Stellenbosch district possessing only a gun.  Opgaaf, 1752.  * Diederick Aucamp came in 1727 to the Cape as a soldier. He was Polish, from Raden. Obtaining burgher rights in 1737, he married and had six children. He lived in the Drakenstein district for thirty years, but planted no crops and possessed no stock. He was obliged to ask for poor relief from the Church Council on account of ‘poverty and ill health’.  LR 1:4; 1752 Opgaaf; 1782 Opgaaf; Hoge, "Personalia", 10.  *

heading: Frontier women
text: Frontier women

text: In the loan farm registers of October 1708 there is a humble but significant complaint filed against two frontiersmen Pieter Erasmus and Barend Blom living near the Vier-en-twinitigrivieren. The complaint is by their neighbour, the widow Elbertz. In her petition, she grumbled that they “lie” too near her. The new governor turned down their applications himself.  CAD. RLR, 1 (1708): folios 170 & 172.  * From the prompt official response it is apparent that the widow, Aletta ter Mollen from Hannover, enjoyed some heft as a landowner. She had been the former spouse of one of the first heemraden in Stellenbosch. Her late husband Heinrich Elbertsz, a German from Osnabruk, was amongst the first group of vrijburghers to be given land on the first frontier, the Liesbeeck valley in 1658. He obtained grazing rights in the Hottentots Holland in 1678. He had acquired several farms in Stellenbosch and applied for a hunting permit in 1689.  It is not clear whether this is the farm referred to in the complaint.  * But the Widow Elbertz had probably established herself on the farm Halfmanshof near Vier-en-twintigrivieren some time beore the official grant was made in 1712.  CAD. RLR, 1-2 (1712-13): passim (new applications); Her son Gerrit also applied for loan farms in the area in 1712 and 1713.  *

text: Because women were always in a numerical minority at the Cape, their voices were heard clearly on the frontier as the Elbertsz episode demonstrates. In the early Cape widows were in a particularly strong position because of the system of joint partible inheritance, through which they inherited half their husbands’ estates and thereby becoming major landowners at the Cape.  Robert C-H Shell, Children of Bondage (Johannesburg: Witwatersrand University Press, 1997), p 209.  * This is also true on the frontier where some widows like Beatrix Verwey became virtual loan farm barons, making a record twenty seven applications for loan farms between 1703 and 1716.

text: The widows of senior officials,were also well represented in the early loan farm registers. Helena Gulix, the widow of Willem Ten Damme, made eleven loan farm applications after her husband’s death from 1714 until 1734. These included grazing lands that he had already acquired at Groenekloof, de Brakkefontein (granted to his widow in 1703) and Kleigat next to Sonquaskloof.  CAD. RLR, 3-9 (1714- 39): passim, (6 new applications, 5 renewals).  * In the VOC map Widow ten Damme’s name appears on the west coast. Willem ten Damme had held the post of Chief Surgeon and was a close friend of the Governor, Willem Adriaan van der Stel, but his wife who was known as “Leen de Schout” was said to be particularly influential with the Governor. One of their daughters, Helena, married the Governor Hendrik Swellengrebel and gave their combined names to the frontier town Swellendam which would briefly even have a republican phase.  DSAB, 4: 644, s.v. "Ten Damme"  *

text: Widows had bargaining power: some like Helena Gulix consolidated their late husbands’ property never marrying again, while others like Elsje Heinrichs van Sürwürden, made three good marriages thereby dramatically improving their lot. Elsje Heinrichs, born in 1662 of a German immigrant father, married Albert Breugel, Junior Merchant in the VOC, then eight years later Andries de Man, the Deputy Governor at the Cape and lastly Hendrik Munkerus, Senior Merchant and Bookkeeper. After his death, Elsje renewed Munkerus’s licence for collecting salt in the Groenekloof in 1706 and obtained grants in her name for the farms De Tygerbergen in 1695 and Rondeboshje in 1705.  CAD. RLR, 1 (1706): folio 146.  *

text: The twice-widowed Christina Stans entered the loan farm market on her own, proceeding to make eight applications between 1710 and 1714 for farms at the Mosselbankrivier, Koeberg and Vishoek, Hottentos Holland, present-day Gordon’s Bay. Her first marriage was to Jan Stevensz Botma (a second generation burgher) and her second marriage to a VOC official, Johan Meerland. She doubled the size of his freehold farm, Meerendal near Tygerberg, with an additional grant in 1712.  CAD. RLR, 1-2 (1710-14): passim (six new applications, two renewals).  *

text: Less known but prominent in the loan farms registers is the widow of Isaac Schrijver, the Ensign who led expeditions to barter with the Khoekhoe in the interior from 1688 - 1697.  Dan Sleigh, Die Buiteposte (Pretoria: Protea Boekhuis, 2004), 67.  * These expeditions took him as far as the Eastern Cape so it is not surprising that he applied for a loan farm at Riviersondered, an area he must have passed through often. Applications and renewals for grazing land in this area were made by his widow twelve times between 1709 and 1722.  CAD RLR, 1 (1709-22): passim (eight new applications, 4 renewals).  * Schrijver’s widow, Anna Hoeks, also retained the Stellenbosch farm, Schoongezicht (now Lanzerac) which he had been granted in 1692.

text: A good example of a knecht marrying a propertied widow is that of Petrus Tavenrath of Rheinberg, tutor for WA van der Stel’s children. In 1711 he became a burger and married Helena Bezuidenhout the widow of Johan Wessels from Hamburg, who had made four hunting applications in the Groenkloof 1706-7. On 23 April 1711 - a scant four days after her wedding to Tavenrath—a loan farm described being at Dassenberg on the Groenerivier is transferred from Helena’s name to that of Tavenrath and renewed in his name until 1712. Helena died in 1713 so it probably reverted to her estate as she had five children by her previous marriage.  Hoge, "Personalia", 420.  *

text: Women sometimes stood together to secure their own and their children’s inheritance. A few matrilineal frontier dynasties evolved: the most spectacular being that of the Verwey family. Tryntjie Theunis, the widow of Gysbert Verwey, farmed initially at Coornhoop and then at Doordekraal near Tygerberg, where she was known as Tryntje de Boerin (Tryntje, the farmer). She dabbled in illegal trade with the Khoekhoe, thereby gaining some knowledge of frontier life.  DSAB, 4: 649, sub verbo "Theunis, T."  * In 1701 Tryntjie’s eldest daughter Beatrix, joined her at Tygerberg after the death of her husband Hendrik Cornelisz Olivier. As widows, both Beatrix and her sister Aletta, who had married Ockert Olivier, settled on farms close to their mother at Klaar Annasfonteyn and De Kleine Stinkrivier. Beatrix Verwey went on to acquire extensive land on the frontier: “in de duynen agter de grauwenheuwel” and “aan de Kleinbergrivier omtrent [het] Land van Waveren”.  CAD RLR, 1-3 (1703-16): passim (ten hunting licences, fifteen new applications, two renewals).  * In the De la Fontaine report of 1731 she is described as “een vrouw de geld heeft”.  Leonard Guelke, Robert Shell, Anthony Whyte, comps., "The de la Fontaine Report" (New Haven: Opgaaf Project, 1990).  * Most convicing of all her name “Beatrix” features twice on the official VOC map of the interior.  Beatrix's daughter, Beatrix Olivier, widow of Pieter van der Westhuizen, obtained the farm Nooit Gedagt in the Swartland in 1744.  *

text: Maria Evertz, the daughter of West African freed-slaves, Evert and Anna of Guinea, became an affluent wine and stock farmer. Having divorced her first husband, a freeblack by the name of Jackie Joy in 1608, she had a long-standing relationship with Bastiaansz Colyn by whom she had five children.  Hans Heese, Groep sonder Grense (Bellville: University Western Cape, 1984), 7.  * She was granted the farm Agter de Cloof at Camps Bay and was one of the first burgheresse to obtain grazing land in the Clavervalley in 1712. After 1713 loan farms at Groenekloof and Sonquasfontein were renewed in the name of the “Erfgename van Maria Evertz” i.e. her heirs.  CAD RLR, 1-3 (1712-15): passim (new applications).  * We may assume that she firmly established a frontier dynasty before the smallpox claimed her.

text: The freeblack, Anna Groothenning, provided a female link in a partnership of three German frontiersmen. Anna who came from Bengal, was the slave of Hans Caspar Geringer, who applied for loan farms at Jan Witjeskraal and “in de duynen”’ in partnership with Christian Bock. In 1709 Geringer manumitted Anna and her children, including one daughter by him, Maria Groothenning, and three children by his partner, Christian Bock. In 1713 Anna married Bock and had two more children. Bock died in 1716 and Geringer took on a new partner, the Swiss, Jacob Marik, by whom Anna also had a son.  Hoge, "Personalia", 36,110,483.  *

text: By offering love, companionship, sex and family life, women from all walks of life helped stabilise frontier society as the border moved forward. In doing this they were the “domesticators” of the interior, to use Davis’ apt neologism for American frontier women. But the Cape frontier women did more than their American counterparts: they established their own personal dominance over large and rugged tracts of land and society. The Cape frontier opened up avenues for an emerging multi ethnic matriarchy which easily matched the frontier patriarchy of our well travelled frontier historiography.

heading: Conclusions
text: Conclusions
html: Conclusions

text: The character of settler expansion and frontier settlement in South Africa is different from the prevailing interpretations of both the ‘entrepreneurial’ and ‘diaspora’ schools of South African frontier history. Internal demographic pressure and economic attractions on the frontier were only minor aspects of the dispersion of European expansion. A strongly fluctuating European economy was pushing wave after wave of unemployed males outwards. Some of these waves broke on South African shores, in turn setting up locally differentiated demographic ripple effects. But whether these immigrants actually opened up the frontier by trade and hunting as they did in 1702, or married peaceably in the arable areas of the Western Cape, their demographic and cultural pressure was felt. Frontier settlement and settler expansion was as much a function of European economic conditions leading to individuated migration and a delayed citizenship as it was of the much exaggerated but to date, imperfectly understood demographic exprience of the original European settlers. The nature of the particular inheritance system at the Cape which was favourable to women provides a key explanation for some of the outstanding differences between the North America and the early Cape frontier experience.
html: The character of settler expansion and frontier settlement in South Africa is different from the prevailing interpretations of both the ‘entrepreneurial’ and ‘diaspora’ schools of South African frontier history. Internal demographic pressure and economic attractions on the frontier were only minor aspects of the dispersion of European expansion. A strongly fluctuating European economy was pushing wave after wave of unemployed males outwards. Some of these waves broke on South African shores, in turn setting up locally differentiated demographic ripple effects. But whether these immigrants actually opened up the frontier by trade and hunting as they did in 1702, or married peaceably in the arable areas of the Western Cape, their demographic and cultural pressure was felt. Frontier settlement and settler expansion was as much a function of European economic conditions leading to individuated migration and a delayed citizenship as it was of the much exaggerated but to date, imperfectly understood demographic exprience of the original European settlers. The nature of the particular inheritance system at the Cape which was favourable to women provides a key explanation for some of the outstanding differences between the North America and the early Cape frontier experience.

text: The rapid growth of historical archaeology, and an expansion of contract archaeology (Cultural Resource Management - CRM) in Cape Town, has coincided with archaeologists, historians and architectural historians becoming more interested in ordinary people and the material culture of the colonial town that was created by its inhabitants.

text: Archives and Archaeology is one of a series of handbooks produced for historical archaeologists. It points a way into and around the documentary resources available for research into Cape households during the colonial periods from about 1700 to 1900. The guidelines will also be of interest to architects and planners and should assist those interested in knowing more about the history of their family, household or neighbourhood.

text: This Guide focuses on Cape Town. We provide an overview of sources available for historic research of Cape Town: where they are located, what information is available, and the level of accessibility (whether computerised or easy to find and use). Investigation of rural properties follows roughly the same procedures, but we indicate points of difference when appropriate.

text: The methodology described for basic archival research has been developed in conjunction with the Archaeology Contracts Office at the University of Cape Town (UCT). We also acknowledge the contribution of Kathy Schulz. A typical request for historical research is one generated by building development in central Cape Town. The brief normally requires preparation of a Phase One Archival Research report. This includes property history and some indication of who lived on the site, whether any material remains do/may survive above-ground and/or may still be traceable below-ground, and whether there are any particularly sensitive areas requiring further preliminary investigation.

text: The pursuit of archaeology in an urban environment is problematic. Our access to subsurface evidence (either below ground or behind paint and plaster) is too often limited to small-scale excavations that reveal dense and complex accumulations of clues that are difficult to untangle and understand without broader contexts. Material culture studies, and the recreation of households (the buildings and the family, servants and slaves), however, can call on a large body of documentary sources. 'hat limited understanding we have gained of earliest colonial domestic architecture Cape Town is still based on the documentary record alone. The mid-eighteenth century onwards, though, has also been traced in standing buildings by systematic excavation' of building fabric as walls are demolished or re-plastered.

Material culture studies, and the recreation of households (the buildings and the family, servants and slaves), however, can call on a large body of documentary sources. 'hat limited understanding we have gained of earliest colonial domestic architecture Cape Town is still based on the documentary record alone. The mid-eighteenth century onwards, though, has also been traced in standing buildings by systematic excavation' of building fabric as walls are demolished or re-plastered.

text: It is unlikely that excavations will take place in blocks where all the standing buildings have already been substantially rebuilt or altered during the twentieth century. Again, therefore, the documentary record is the basis on which our understanding their history will lie. But there are also problems with the documentary record, which is patchy over time, often incomplete, and biased towards over- or under-representing certain categories of places or people. Even with the combination of a number of sources, a block's inhabitants and their dwellings remain elusive.

text: It is useful to have a spatial framework, in the form of contemporary plans, on which to hang information from a variety of sources. The nineteenth century surveys are teal, and the mid-eighteenth century is well represented in Wentzel's plan. Some of the most versatile documents are probate records, in particular household inventories. In cases where more that one appraisal was made of a single household, changes trough time can be revealed. Where more than one inventory was taken in the study area within the same period, comparisons can be made between different households.

text: There are two major publications dealing with documentary sources for historical archaeologists (both North American) available at Jagger Library, UCT: Documentary Archaeology in the New World edited by Mary Beaudry (1988) and ext-Aided Archaeology edited by Barbara J. Little (1992). They are collections of papers selected to demonstrate the use of the historical record by archaeologists to answer archaeological questions.

text: Mary Beaudry points out that archaeologists necessarily focus on material culture (buildings, cultural landscapes, potsherds, and so on) with a bias towards `what happened in the past', unlike historians who see history as `the act of selecting, analyzing, and writing about the past'. Both historians and archaeologists agree on the need to read the documentary evidence critically, but their research strategies will be different (Beaudry 1988:1-3). There are books on methodology written to help the archaeologist analyse and interpret excavated materials, but not many focus on the use of historical documentation for the archaeologist, or on particular ways to use various texts.

There are books on methodology written to help the archaeologist analyse and interpret excavated materials, but not many focus on the use of historical documentation for the archaeologist, or on particular ways to use various texts.

text: A rapid growth of historical archaeology as a sub-discipline, and an expansion of contract archaeology, has coincided with historians and architects increasingly seeking information on the material context of daily colonial life. Here and elsewhere this has lead to a growing recognition that history and anthropology (the umbrella discipline of archaeology) need each other: a trend towards `historical anthropology or anthropological history', as Barbara Little terms it (Little 1992:1-2). Archaeologists interpret material culture, and material culture includes representations and remnants of culture, both objects and texts.

text: There is a useful review of sources available to the historical archaeologist described by Mary Ellin D'Agostino (1995), in which she points to the need for generalised comparisons to be grounded in and informed by context, structure, and “situatedness” (detailed and deep “local knowledge”). Working with these records, however, requires "a concerted, time consuming effort to become familiar with new sets of data, their strengths and weaknesses, and to apply them to archaeological goals" (D'Agostino 1995:120).

heading: Computer applications
text: Computer applications
html: Computer applications

text: Computer applications in history include both quantitative and qualitative approaches. Textual analysis is especially problematic because of the need to record inconsistently written manuscripts in a systematic way, if the researcher wishes to go beyond the extremes of literal transcription or tabular information. Thomas Lindblad (1990) has written helpfully on these issues. At a fundamental level he differentiates between three successive stages in processing information. Firstly, the researcher records a data set of raw data taken directly from the source in a machine-readable form. Next a data base is constructed so as to allow further analysis. Then, the processed file may be integrated into a larger collection of data files to form part of a data bank for wider future use.

text: There is a serious lack of computerised information based on Cape colonial archives, except the system accessed through the computer at the Archives itself. In the course of Antonia Malan's research a data set of property transfers, household inventories and other probate records is gradually becoming expanded, and data bases are being set up for particular properties. Transcribed indexes are being lodged in the National Archives (CA) as soon as they are prepared. The standard used is the Microsoft Office package because it is widely available. There are some local web pages associated with historical archaeology, architectural history and heritage management, such as www.uct.ac.za/depts/age  or www.heritage.org.za.

text: The initial task for research into a property, block or area of Cape Town is to look at the property surviving buildings and context - then to trace the history of the piece of  land. The first house erven (plots) in Cape Town were formally granted on 20  September 1660, on which day eight such grants were issued. As the property was  passed from one owner to the next, the history of owners or occupiers can be  followed up and the story of the buildings and their uses described. In the following sub-sections we describe the sources we use and where they are to be found in Cape Town: property transfers and surveys; maps and plans; probate records; architecture; graphics; the people - social history; street directories, almanacs and newspapers.

text: These instructions were given by Rijkloff van Goens to Jan van Riebeeck, who passed them on to Pieter Potter (lantmeter ende kaertmaeker) in 1657 (Fisher 1984:57). We see in the general plans and the title diagrams drafted by Potter a system of recording rights in land which, in principle, is exactly the same as that which we use today. text: C. Graham Botha wrote “Early Cape Land Tenure” for the South African Law Journal of 1919 and it remains an excellent source (see also Pretorius 1997:208). There were three distinct forms of land tenure under VOC administration: Loan (leening), Quitrent (erfpacht) and Freehold (eigendom). Of these the freehold and quitrent tenures were subject to formal registration by title deed. Loan tenure was only sometimes recorded in title deeds with surveyor's diagrams.

Of these the freehold and quitrent tenures were subject to formal registration by title deed. Loan tenure was only sometimes recorded in title deeds with surveyor's diagrams.

text: The first freeburgher colonists were granted land along the Liesbeek River in 1657.
html: The first freeburgher colonists were granted land along the Liesbeek River in 1657.

text: Before then, small garden plots in Table Valley were held on loan and permits were granted to graze cattle in certain places. After 1714 holders of loan places paid tithes to the Government. A loan place was given out after an individual petitioned for the right to occupy the land, giving a name of some spring or spot round which the property was situated. Hence many farm names end in —fontein.
html: Before then, small garden plots in Table Valley were held on loan and permits were granted to graze cattle in certain places. After 1714 holders of loan places paid tithes to the Government. A loan place was given out after an individual petitioned for the right to occupy the land, giving a name of some spring or spot round which the property was situated. Hence many farm names end in —fontein.

text: In 1732 quitrent tenure was introduced. It was a grant of land for 15 years on payment of an annual rent. After 1743 it became possible to convert loan places into loan freehold or perpetual loans (leenings-eigendom). A loan freehold place was to be 60 morgen in extent and represented by a diagram. A rent of 24 rixdollars was paid in addition to a fee on delivery of the Title Deed (erfgrondbrief). In some districts there was also a custom that allowed the farmer to take a measurement from a central spot, such as homestead, spring or rock formation, and “occupy three hours’ ground round the middle of his place, that is, half an hour on every side of the same” (ordonnantie). The ‘walking off’ distance was regarded as about 750 roods which resulted in an area of 3000 morgen.

After 1743 it became possible to convert loan places into loan freehold or perpetual loans (leenings-eigendom). A loan freehold place was to be 60 morgen in extent and represented by a diagram. A rent of 24 rixdollars was paid in addition to a fee on delivery of the Title Deed (erfgrondbrief). In some districts there was also a custom that allowed the farmer to take a measurement from a central spot, such as homestead, spring or rock formation, and “occupy three hours’ ground round the middle of his place, that is, half an hour on every side of the same” (ordonnantie). The ‘walking off’ distance was regarded as about 750 roods which resulted in an area of 3000 morgen.

text: Freehold grants, although made ‘in full and free property’ (vollen en vrijen eijgendom), carried various conditions such as erection of suitable buildings, payment of tithes, provision of access and thoroughfares, cultivation of the land, planting and replacement of felled trees, and so on. The VOC Government retained overall control of loan properties. Under loan tenure the occupier could not sell the property but could sell or bequeath the opstallen or buildings on the farm.

The VOC Government retained overall control of loan properties. Under loan tenure the occupier could not sell the property but could sell or bequeath the opstallen or buildings on the farm.

text: In 1813 Cradock's Law reformed the whole system. The law was intended to increase the security of loan property holders to encourage them to invest in land and to improve it. They could also dispose of it as they wished. These grants were known as Perpetual Quitrent (eeuwigdurende erfpacht). Lands on this tenure were surveyed and a lease with a diagram was recorded, a duplicate being issued to the lessee. The transfer of immovable property held in ownership took place before the Commissioners of the Court of Justice up to 1828, after which it was before the Registrar of Deeds, a newly created office. Freehold and perpetual quitrent grants became the two forms of Cape land tenure throughout the nineteenth century.

text: At the office of the Surveyor General and Deeds Office (SGO, DO) in Plein Street, Cape Town, land grants, individual property surveys and deeds of transfer are stored.
html: At the office of the Surveyor General and Deeds Office (SGO, DO) in Plein Street, Cape Town, land grants, individual property surveys and deeds of transfer are stored.

text: Documents in volumes called Old Cape Freehold (OCF) and Old Stellenbosch Freehold (OSF) record the official registration of the original grant of freehold land. Similar volumes record the Quitrent grants. The history of the ownership of properties can be followed up from initial grant to the present-day. Occasionally, survey plans indicate details of the shape of houses, outbuildings and other features, as well as the grounds surrounding them.

text: The first three volumes of OCFs were all redrawn and rewritten at some stage, so some originals are kept at the Cape Archives as well. The volumes are incredibly beautiful art objects but people can still use them with no supervision. Besides naming the owner and describing the configuration and boundaries of grants, they mention neighbours, show some landscape features and sometimes give obligations of ownership, like erecting hedges or keeping watercourses free running. Very occasionally they show the outline of buildings and even more occasionally there is a description of the circumstances of the grant. Owners also got a copy of the grant or re-grant and these sometimes turn up in private collections. For instance the owners of Leeuwenhof have an OCF re-grant diagram on which the house at the time was drawn. All OCFs have the first subsequent transfer noted, taking you straight to the transfer deeds (see below).

text: Another procedure is to locate the Noting Sheet that covers the area in question, on the 9th floor of the SGO. This indicates the current erf numbers of the properties in the block. The earliest Noting Sheet for Cape Town was the ‘Cape Rood’ map of circa 1901, which has been lost. Some original Noting Sheets date to the 1930s, and these have relatively more buildings shown on them. The circa 1930 series of printed maps were based on the Cape Times "hundred foot sheets" (100 Cape feet: 1 inch). They were redrawn and filed with the SGO. Tracings, by M.S. Lacock, were made from second or third-hand versions. The originals covering central Table Valley have been destroyed, but some still exist for peripheral areas. The modem `dummy files', i.e. sheets redrawn for the SGO, are also unsatisfactorily archived. Houses and many minor details and features were not recorded on redrawn maps.

text: These show amalgamations on a modern ground plan. Caution is required when using these documents, as erf numbers can differ from the original ones. Dates on the diagrams are not always of the first grant, but often the date of first subdivision. This especially relates to farm registers, where researchers are often misled into believing that the first diagram date was date of first occupation. Only town centre properties on Old (Cape or Stellenbosch) Freehold (OCF or OSF) numbers can be trusted to be earliest grants, and in rare cases even these grants may be re-grants made to resolve a dispute. In upper Table Valley there are countless examples of earlier `first' grants which require imaginative searching and a modicum of luck to track down.

text: General information can be obtained from the 12th floor office. If you intend to spend time working with primary documents, rather than merely request copies of the property history, you will need to seek permission from the Director to go into the strong rooms.

text: Leonard Guelke and Robert Shell (1990) were pioneers in compiling computerised indexes. Their Deeds Book is one starting place for locating early property transfers and subsequent transfers (up to 1732). There is a copy in the Cape Archives on which corrections have been made, but it is always wise to check information in the original manuscripts. For Cape Town, there are also plans showing the grants and TD numbers of each property (see section on Maps and Plans).

text: From present erf numbers (or, in the case of rural estates, district and farm numbers) an abbreviated history of the property can be found bound in numerically ordered files, housed on the 14th floor of the SGO. The first grant is usually noted, or previous erf number if it is a deduction, and then a selection of subsequent property transfers and deductions. Alternatively, there is a hand written volume that lists transfers by year (Register of property transfers). This volume still needs to be transcribed onto computer, though there is a microfilm in existence.

text: It is then possible to trace each transfer from original grant to the present day, in transfer deed manuscripts filed by date in the strong rooms on the 13th floor. Each deed of transfer should contain dates of previous transfers in the text and is cross-written with the next transfer number and date. If the next transfer information is missing or difficult to decipher, skip to the next document listed in the abbreviated history volume and then work backward to fill in the gap.

text: Researching property in both the Deeds Registry and in the Cape Archives has revealed the existence in the latter repository of owners of particular properties whose names do not appear in the Deeds Registry as registered owners of those properties. Historical accuracy demands that these persons be included in any compilation of any property history even if their legal position as owners is not clearly defined or established. What is important from the historical angle is that they did exist as de facto owners ... The vast proportion of these owners were spouses married in community of property who, as such, had a right to registered ownership but, in those circumstances and during the period under review, registration was not demanded.... Sometimes, in successive transfer deeds the transferee and transferor do not coincide. This can result from a single marriage in community of property so the transferor is the widow of the transferee. But community of property was the norm in all but a very small proportion of marriages during the Dutch period. A single marriage for a person was also unusual. The consequent devolvement of immovable property under this combination of circumstances produced an array of unregistered owners that the Court of Justice initially did nothing to control. Testate and intestate heirs who were not husband and wife formed an added complication and in quite a few cases escaped registration entirely. Since these factors are interwoven with family histories the search involves church registers, wills, kinderbewysen, inventories, accounts and sales of deceased estates, insolvencies and census returns. However, the date of someone's death need not necessarily be registered before 1759.

text: Deceased estates and complex inheritance details therefore often result in unrecorded subdivisions. Short-term events within the family are not always reflected in the transfers. A good example is Pieter van Breda who was shown living at Nooitgedacht (now St Cyprians School) in a drawing of circa 1803 at Koopmans de Wet house (see Harris 1998a & 1998b). The property was ‘owned’ at the time by 10 Versfeld van Breda's late wife's late previous husband. The sale of a property could take place months and sometimes years before the Deed was processed. The supporting leaflets and bonds sometimes give information about this.

text: Transfers record the owner's name and spouse, legal ownership or title, price, occupation, neighbours, etc. They do not record occupants (except rarely) or details of intra-family ownership. The receipt for transfer duty is a useful document for cross checking illegible information, such as names. Care should be taken to avoid mistaking bonds for transfers. Where there is no cross-writing (details of the next transfer), check the previous deed that had a survey diagram with it and look for attached notes of subdivision or amalgamation, which will list the name and date of next transfer.

heading: Maps and plans

text: In 1997 the Research Unit for the Archaeology of Cape Town (RESUNACT) inaugurated a Historic Maps Working Group. The Group's activities include the compilation of lists of resources at the various archival institutions of Cape Town, digitisation of maps and plans, reproductions of commonly used materials, and lobbying for proper care and attention to be paid to non-renewable resources. Once the Historic Maps Working Group has completed an inventory of map holdings in Cape Town, this will be made available to researchers.

text: The Survey Department of the City Council of Cape Town (CCC) has an invaluable collection of historic maps and plans of the city, as well as many extending colony and country wide. The collection was established by Ralph Taylor, and since his death has been overseen by Ian Black. They are not freely accessible, however. The Cape Archives also stores original copies of maps and plans, old maps from the Surveyor General's Office, as well as photographs and prints of maps and plans. The South African Library (SAL) and the African Studies Library at UCT (ASL) have further items in their collections. Another source of plans useful for locating addresses are in published Street Directories.

heading: Wentzel
text: Wentzel
html: Wentzel

text: Carel David Wentzel was the colony's surveyor from 1749 to 1759. He came to the Cape in 1748 and married Aurelia Stavorinus in 1751. Repatriated in 1760 he later returned as an engineer officer of the Dutch East India Company. His plan of Cape Town, ca 1750, is valuable because of the details of subdivisions within many of the blocks, showing lot shapes and numbers; and there is a list of `new' wardmasters attached. The plan was probably commissioned to record and control the expansion of a fast-growing and increasingly dense settlement. It is widely reproduced in original and traced form. A clear A3 reproduction is in Gentleman's Walk (Picard 1968:38).

heading: Thibault
text: Thibault
html: Thibault

text: The career of Louis Michel Thibault (engineer and surveyor 1783-1815) is relatively well documented. Of general interest is the survey of Crown land along the new road from Woodstock to Wynberg, started in 1811 and completed in 1813. Thibault's preliminary setting-out surveys of both sides of the road are at the Cape Archives in a series starting M1/191. His original plan of the western (or right) side of the road was copied by the Surveyor-General before being sent to the State Archives for safekeeping (CA: M3/41). The copy became filed as General Plan (registration) No. 639K (6973). The plan of the eastern (or left) side of the road is a partly completed pencil plot filed in the Surveyor-General's office as General Plan No.917. In 1977 a compilation plan combining the two plans was prepared in the Land Survey office of the City Engineer's Department, CCC (Sims 1997).

text: In the Kaapse Plakaatboek for 1787-1795, under 27 December 1793 to 16 January 1784, Abraham Josias Sluysken demarcated ward numbers (Margaret Cairns pers. comm.). A plan of Cape Town possibly surveyed by Thibault at the end of the eighteenth century remains today in the form of a small framed water-colour, part of the William Fehr Collection. It shows the names of streets and landmarks and some occupants. De Puyfontaine (1972) does not enlarge on the minimal information contained in the figure caption to the plan in her book on Thibault, but a contemporaneous census taken of the inhabitants of Cape Town appears strongly connected (see section on Census Rolls). The numbers of the wards are identical, and the listed inhabitants include those shown on the plan as the occupants of corner plots.

heading: Jones

text: Josephus Jones worked in the Cape between 1784 and 1811. He came as an artillery man but proved to be an experienced mapmaker and draughtsman (Gordon-Brown 1975:251). See the section on Graphics, below, for a discussion of his panorama which belongs to the Rembrandt Art Foundation, Stellenbosch. There was a poorly focused, reversed (negative) print of the map he made of Table Valley in the Cape Archives (CA; M3/117), but now there is also a laser photocopy reversal of this. The Rijksarchief in The Hague were unable to find their copy when it was requested in 1996. This map is important because, apart from the untrustworthy Eleman's map of 1818, it is the only one that charts the early expansion of Cape Town outside its eighteenth century boundaries and has good information on Upper Table Valley.

text: William Barclay Snow completed a “Plan of the Municipalities of Cape Town, Greenpoint & Seapoint” in 1862. He offered to do a survey of Cape Town in 1861 but the authorities declined to commission it. He finally went ahead anyway and produced a 4,2 by 3,7 metre plan at a scale of 1 inch to 10 Cape roods. It shows all buildings with specific reference to churches, military and government buildings, as well as all topographical and cadastral information (Sims 1997). The result is regarded as being accurate and immensely useful. He even inspected (and seems to have measured) back yards.

heading: Wilson
text: Wilson
html: Wilson

text: Alexander Wilson made his map of Cape Town for the Cape of Good Hope Gas Light Company in 1860. The version usually cited was dated 1878 (now housed at Surveys and Land Information, CCC). The map is especially valuable because it shows the layout of gardens at the time, of agricultural holdings and suburban villas. Unfortunately, the map was painted with varnish that has turned dark brown. After 45 years as the Manager of Cape Town's Gas Works, Alexander Wilson died in 1890 and was buried at St Peter's Church, Mowbray.

After 45 years as the Manager of Cape Town's Gas Works, Alexander Wilson died in 1890 and was buried at St Peter's Church, Mowbray.

text: According to the Cape Argus of 31 January 1860, Wilson's "superb topographical map was intended originally for the service of the company, in exhibiting the extent to which their gas pipes are laid, but it comprises now far more than this, and presents a most accurate picture of the whole valley from the sea to the slopes of Table Mountain, giving the mountain streams and water leadings with great precision". Wilson's map was re- issued in 1872 as The Topographical Plan of Cape Town and Suburbs, now including "the Railway Works, new Docks, Harbour improvements, telegraphs; and every new building in town and suburbs has been added up to the present date". The revised map included: "to the south of town the village of Papendorp and all properties on Rondebosch Road as far as Altona Station; the whole of Table Valley to the top of the Mountain; all blocks sub-divided showing every house and store; to the north the whole of Green Point Municipality, with Tramways and Water Works; extended to all properties in Camp's Bay as far as the south side of Stinkwater valley; every source of water supply is shown with levels". The scale of the map is 200 feet to the inch, and it measures loft 6inches by 8ft (Worth 1996).

heading: Thom
text: Thom
html: Thom

text: Walter Thom was brought from England to the Cape on contract to the Municipal Council of Cape Town in 1891. Thom's survey dates to circa 1898, but he surveyed the area over a period of time, starting in 1894, so the dates of sheets differ. The sheets around Schoonekloof date to 1895, and the streets of central Tamboerskloof date to mid- 1899. The map sheets are extremely clear and detailed, down to the shape of stoep steps and garden layout in some cases. He had been instructed to include reliable information on the situation of all water main, drains, sewers, etc. There is a key plan at a scale of 1 inch to 500 English feet or 1:6000 and 134 sheets at a scale of 1 inch to 50 English feet. The original plans are stored in the archives of the Survey and Land Information branch of the CCC (Sims 1997).

heading: Building plans
text: Building plans
html: Building plans

text: From 1887 the various Municipalities around Cape Town required plans of buildings and alterations to be submitted for approval, at first patchily complied with, but a  sequence which continues until today. They show plans, sections and elevations of  the structures, signatures of owner and architect, key location maps and indicate  materials. The originals are at CA (until circa 1965) with the rest and complete microfiches at CCC. There is an index to them at Jagger Library (Manuscripts and Archives), now also on computer at the Urban Conservation Unit, CCC. The index, made by Professor Pryce-Lewis, covers the period to 1913 for all Municipalities,  except Wynberg, the size of which defeated him. The index is accessible by street name, owner, architect and plan number. Access to building plans for people other than the building's owner is not permitted at present.

heading: Probate records

html: Probate records

text: A basic motivation for Antonia Malan's material culture studies is to systematically build up detailed records from probate records lodged in the Archives in Roeland Street (CA). Inventories & Appraisals of Estates, and Auction lists of loose goods subsequently sold off, are filed with the papers of the Master of the Orphan Chamber (MOOCS and MOOC10 respectively). Under colonial governments during the eighteenth and early nineteenth century, the Orphan Chamber was responsible for intestate estates and the affairs of minors and widows. The list below was transcribed directly from the Finding Aids lodged in the Archives, with asterisks added to indicate those records that have been indexed on computer.

Estate Papers, 1688-1800, vols. 2914-2951; and (x) Registers & Indexes to Notarial Documents, 1702-1779, vol. 3135. The Stellenbosch District has its own files of inventories: 1/STB. Rural and dorp inventories filed under Stellenbosch papers 1/STB are in volumes 18/30-39, dating from 1687 to 1827. Volumes 18/37 onwards have an index.

heading: Indexes

text: The procedure was first to computerise some hand written indexes for these sources. The early indexes are notably difficult to use in their original forms as the people are listed alphabetically by first name rather than surname. A decision was made to use a word processor programme (rather than spreadsheet or database), so that as many people as possible working in the archives would have access to them. They can then be sorted by name, by spouse or heir, by location and by date. Room-by-room inventories have been partially indexed as part of doctoral research (Malan 1993), and a copy of the thesis is lodged with the Archives. Since then, with the advent of Microsoft Windows, the indexes need to be converted.

heading: Household inventories and auctions
text: Household inventories and auctions
html: Household inventories and auctions

text: Selected documents have been transcribed in detail. Because of difficulties in working with fragile manuscripts, which cannot be photocopied, it was necessary to transcribe directly from the original documents into the computer. As a crucial adjunct to the work, therefore, these computerised records become available to researchers so that the originals can remain untouched.
html: Selected documents have been transcribed in detail. Because of difficulties in working with fragile manuscripts, which cannot be photocopied, it was necessary to transcribe directly from the original documents into the computer. As a crucial adjunct to the work, therefore, these computerised records become available to researchers so that the originals can remain untouched.

text: In brief, household inventories are a list of assets compiled by approved appraisers, most commonly after the death of a householder (man or woman). The purpose of the appraisal was to ensure fair distribution of the estate to heirs, not just for tax purposes. Not all households were inventoried, however, so it is a matter of luck if the focus of research, such as a house or family, was inventoried. These records vary in size and quality, from a very sparse list of possessions to many pages listing several hundred items described room-by-room and including extensive stores.
html: In brief, household inventories are a list of assets compiled by approved appraisers, most commonly after the death of a householder (man or woman). The purpose of the appraisal was to ensure fair distribution of the estate to heirs, not just for tax purposes. Not all households were inventoried, however, so it is a matter of luck if the focus of research, such as a house or family, was inventoried. These records vary in size and quality, from a very sparse list of possessions to many pages listing several hundred items described room-by-room and including extensive stores.

text: The documents are regarded as fair reflections of actual household material culture, as well as being artefacts themselves. The list included landed property, goods and chattels, slaves and livestock, investments, debts and credits of the estate. Because household contents (furniture, clothing, ornaments, and so on) were sometimes listed room-by-room, not only are the material possessions of the household described, but their relationship to each other and the function of the rooms in which they lay is embedded in the documents. House layout can also be schematically reconstructed from the position of the rooms (left/right, back/front, upper/lower) and sequence of appraisal. However, if a room had nothing in it, it may not be listed. This is especially important with regard to slave quarters, which are seldom mentioned, or perhaps this was because their contents belonged to the slaves. Small details, like the number of curtains in a room, can indicate architectural features such as the number of windows, or hearth utensils and over-mantels can indicate the presence of a fireplace.

text: Household inventories are invaluable sources of contextual information about house layout, room function, items of material culture, household inhabitants, status and wealth. They are a frozen moment in the life span of the household. Subsequent auction of the assets of an estate provides another picture of the same household, as the items are dispersed into the community. A description of the object, who purchased it, and the purchase price, are noted. Relative values of items of material culture, and the social dynamics of public auctions in colonial life, are revealed in these documents. See Malan 1993, 1997 and 1998 for more details.

heading: Architecture

text: The building itself is the primary source ‘document’—how it looks, how it is constructed—and will be investigated by conservation architects and archaeologists in Phase One studies. During restoration work on buildings, architects or-builders are not obliged to keep systematic records of their work, unlike obligatory reports for the excavation permit system imposed by the NMC on archaeologists. The granting of demolition permits by the City Council does not require prior architectural recording. Though conservation projects are thoroughly researched by architects, the fruits of their labour are not always accessible. However, many such studies are lodged voluntarily in the NMC library a rich resource.

text: Photographic records or video shots of work in progress (when plaster is stripped off, features revealed, etc.) in particular are useful aids for researching and understanding past histories of buildings. For inspiration read Stewart Brand's How Buildings Learn: What Happens After They're Built (1997). It is an American study of cultural layering using successive photographs to show the changes made to buildings over time, which he employs to develop his theme: the dynamic of change.

text: A thorough building-by-building survey of the City Centre, docks and Bo-Kaap is published as Buildings of Cape Town (BoCT: see References) which has a general introduction to architectural development 1852-1978. text: Old buildings that had managed to survive reasonably intact to 1980 are located and described in Fransen & Cook (1980) albeit the more important ones. They have pieces on materials of the period and the development of Cape architecture from about 1750 to 1850. Mary Cook provided notes from her records for individual house histories (original grant, owners, and so on) but there are a significant number of errors so it is advisable to check original sources. Their first version (The Old Houses of the Cape published in 1965) has been indexed by owner, and can be found on the open shelves of the SA Library [R 720.9687 FRA].

text: Some of the more significant architectural landmarks and elements of late eighteenth and early nineteenth century Cape Town can be found in Ronald Lewcock's book, Early Nineteenth Century Architecture in South Africa (1963), which is extensively illustrated with period graphics and well referenced. The thesis on which the book was based is a little fuller and has glossy original photographs pasted in to it, and can be found in the library of the School of Architecture at UCT.

text: The architectural history of the Victorian years (1838-1901) is described by Dennis Radford (1979) who deals with social and economic impulses, shows influences and describes period detail and construction. Désirée Picton-Seymour's Victorian Buildings in South Africa (1977) describes the buildings of the late colonial period (particularly 1890-1910) and has good pieces on materials, especially cast iron.

text: Publications on rural architecture are considerably more numerous, the better known being James Walton's books, including Homesteads and Villages of South Africa (1965), Old Cape Farmsteads (1989), and Cape Cottages (1995). For those interested in hinges and carpentry, get Obholzer, Baraitser & Malherbe (1985) The Cape House and its Interior. The main source for the history of the Stellenbosch district is still Francois Smuts (1979) Stellenbosch Three Centuries. Architectural developments in Stellenbosch itself are recorded from an archaeological viewpoint in Hennie Vos's MA dissertation, “An historical and archaeological perspective of colonial Stellenbosch, 1680-1860” (1993). There are a number of studies of individual dorps such as Tulbagh (Fagan 1974) and Montagu (Japha 1992).

text: There are considerable numbers of pictures of Cape Town buildings at various stages of growth (and even more can be seen in panoramas, covered later). The problem is finding them many are catalogued by artist rather than general location. Gordon-Brown's Pictorial Africana (1975) references 1000 Cape artists active to the end of the nineteenth century with selected examples of their work. R.F. Kennedy (1966, 1975) catalogued pictures (seven volumes) and prints (two volumes) at MuseumAfrika to 1966, arranged by artist and with an index of places. Picture collections (William Fehr, Library of Parliament) have card indexes. There are several well illustrated publications dealing with individual artists who liked to paint buildings and places, such as Bell, Bowler and D'Oyly.

heading: Panoramas
text: Panoramas

text: Panoramas are wonderful sources to consult, though not all buildings can be expected to have been included by the artist in paintings, and nearly all photographs post-date the mid-nineteenth century. The best-known drawn panoramas are those of Schumacher (1767) who was artist to Swellengrebel, Gordon (1777), the originals of which are in The Netherlands, and the one by Josephus Jones (ca 1808), which can be seen in Stellenbosch.

text: There is a list of all known drawn or painted panoramas of the Table Valley, by Pauline Cook (1959), on the open shelves of the SA Library [RC. 968.700 84 COO (FOL)]. Photographed panoramas can be located in the indexes to photographic collections (but search synonyms, e.g. ‘aerial view’). Secure the Shadow (Bull & Denfield, 1970) is a history of Victorian photographers [R.770.9687 BUL]. Aerial photographs, available from the Trigonometrical Survey Office in Mowbray, were taken at regular intervals from 1926. The first co-ordinated aerial photography in Cape Town was flown in 1936. This covered all the urban and suburban development at a scale of 1:6000. In 1951 additional city-wide coverage at 1:6000 was flown and used to produce uncontrolled mosaics (Sims 1997). The most recent aerial survey was in 1996.

heading: The people: Social History
text: The people: Social History
html: The people: Social History

text: Probate records, genealogies, street directories or almanacs and census rolls are used to trace information about the occupants of the research area. The ordinary inhabitants of colonial Cape Town are difficult enough to track down to particular blocks or buildings, but servants and slaves are almost invisible. Census-taking in the colony was erratic and irregular, genealogies are biased towards elite white males whose lives were recorded by officialdom, and street directories only began to be published in the nineteenth century. The secondary publications of archivists, such as Jeffrey’s (1926), (1964), Leibbrandt (1989) and Thom (1958), provide the major entry into early official records. There are 35 volumes of Theal's Records on open shelves in the SA Library [R 968.7 THE] (and 1964). The reliability and biases of these sources still need to be thoroughly assessed and critiqued, though. The Reference section in this Guide cites those volumes containing indexes.

text: There are a number of excellent more recently published history books and articles about Cape Town. Articles published by archivists and historians provide some glimpses of who lived where at certain times (for instance, Cairns 1974). Worden, van Heyningen & Bickford-Smith (1998 and 1999) have produced the most comprehensive illustrated history of Cape Town. J.L. Hastings’s article (1984:46-49) on early freeblack property-owners in Table Valley provides information about many lesser-known property owners. Margaret Cairns' published works are numerous, but scattered among minor publications, so we prepared a bibliography of some of her articles for the newsletter of the Historical Archaeology Research Group, Crossmend, 1994. After about 1840 the number of newspapers increased, but references to people, businesses and noteworthy events in most areas prove to be sparse and time-consuming to trace.

heading: Probate records

text: A family's structure can be recreated by using the information about heirs included in deceased estate inventories. The head of household, spouse, children and heirs are usually listed. Slaves are listed with the possessions. Names, ages and other incidental snippets about the household can be gleaned by careful reading of inventories and wills.

heading: Genealogies
text: Genealogies
html: Genealogies

text: The main published sources for family histories are De Villagers & Pama (1981), covering well-documented male heads of households who left heirs (stamvaders, and J. Hpge (1946) who concentrated on immigrants of German extraction. Cor Pama edited an updated version of C.C. de Villiers’s original work, Genealogies of Old South African Families (1981), which includes introductory essays on sources. Heese & Lombard (1986 to date) are improving upon De Villiers & Pama by working systematically through the alphabet. Volume 12 is their most recent publication (2005) and covers S0-Sz. Philip (1981) covers British residents at the Cape from 1795 to 1819.

text: Individual family histories can be consulted where necessary. There is an active Genealogical Society in Cape Town that publishes Familia. Hans Heese (1984), working with the deliberate intention of revealing the complex relationships between immigrant Europeans and their bondsmen- and women, has added a significant amount of information about non-elite families. The articles of Margaret Cairns, also covering less well-documented families and women, have been mentioned in the section on archivists. Slave and freeblack genealogies were the particular concern of Anna Boeseken (1977) and Margaret Cairns, and have been gradually built up over the years of publication of Kronos, mouthpiece of the Institute for Historical Research at the University of the Western Cape. More prominent personages can be found in the Dictionary of South African Biography (volumes 1-5) and its successor, the New Dictionary of South African Biography (volumes 1-2).

text: The opgaven list heads of households and the number of people in the family, servants and slaves, and stock, located by district but not the address of the household. For upper Table Valley there are three opgaven - around 1800, 1805 and 1807 - which have been partially transcribed by Harris. He sought information about market gardens and found the estimates of size roughly right, but several people are missing, among them a major land owner, Michiel van Breda, in 1805. Garden names are given in 1800 and 1805.

text: A useful census of central Cape Town contains a ‘List of Persons Living in Wards ... in 1799’ (see section on Maps and Plans for an associated plan). This set of documents is a particularly important resource, because not only does it list the head of the household and his or her family members at a particular address, but also names other occupants such as lodgers and tenants and their servants and slaves. The manuscript is still being fully transcribed, and some wards are missing, but information can be found in the original mss (CA: BRD 27) on Wards 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 13, 15, 19, 20 and 21. The Department of History at UCT is also working on a census from the same period. From this type of source it can be seen that a mere listing of property owners and their families in no way reflects the number or range of inhabitants of a household (see Cairns 1981).

heading: Street Directories, Almanacs & Newspapers
text: Street Directories, Almanacs & Newspapers
html: Street Directories, Almanacs & Newspapers

text: Initially, when the settlement was a small-scale community, addresses and directions given to visitors were based on the names of householders, despite the allocation of street names. In this way, the house or garden-land of a person often took his name (Picard 1968:25-27). The original block lettering and erf numbering system was established early on for locating land grants and tracing subdivisions in transfer deeds, and it was still cited in transfer deeds into the nineteenth century. Maps and plans indicate that expansion of the town lead to additional block and lot numbering (when the alphabet ran out) and ward or district numbering. These numbers, however, changed over time.

text: Street names were only officially marked with signboards in 1790 (Picard 1968:90). Naturally, street names have changed over the years.

text: The earliest published directory, listed by street, was compiled by Eric Rosenthal (1969) from the 1800 census (CA: J37) and has been extended by Heese (1983). This can be compared to previous sources, such as BRD27, also dating to about 1800.
html: The earliest published directory, listed by street, was compiled by Eric Rosenthal (1969) from the 1800 census (CA: J37) and has been extended by Heese (1983). This can be compared to previous sources, such as BRD27, also dating to about 1800.

text: The first contemporary printed list of residents is dated 1810 but until the end of the century they were not listed in street order. The most comprehensive is De Lima's 1855 Almanac for which he claimed he had “not left unvisited a single house, situated in any nook or corner, street, gracht, lane, passage, court or yard” (Worden et al 1998:159). The African Studies Library (in conjunction with the Historical Archaeology Research Group) at the University of Cape Town is working on a major digitization project of the Directories and Almanacs. Every fifth year from 1810 to 1875 has been completed and these records are included in this publication.

text: Gaps in the computerised records can be filled directly from the printed directories and assessment rolls (CA: 3/CT) from other years. A full set of Directories and Almanacs, 1800-1902, are on the open shelves at SAL and others can be called up. In our experience some properties can be difficult to trace because of vagaries in the original sources, changing street numbering over the years and the lack of a significant landmark on or near the block from which to work out street numbers. The names of owners, occupiers, and proprietors of businesses do not always correlate across other records.

text: The original Cape Town Gazette and African Advertiser from August 1800 to October 1801, has been reproduced and indexed by the South African Library (1982). In general, though, newspaper sources do not often contribute very useful information on the material culture of particular households, unless a property is advertised for sale or auction, when its attributes may be fulsomely described.
